# libtmux for Erlang
Create tmux sessions, windows and panes from Erlang. Capture their object graph, filter it as immutable data, and execute source queries and owned operations explicitly. ## Install Use Erlang/OTP **29.1.2**, Rebar3 **3.28.0**, Linux, tmux **3.3a–3.8**, and `make` with a C11 compiler. Native records are experimental in OTP 29. The core uses OTP libraries and a compiled external helper, with no NIF or third-party runtime packages. This checkout is unreleased. Add its core application to your `rebar.config`: ```erlang {deps, [ {libtmux_erlang, {git_subdir, "https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang.git", {branch, "master"}, "apps/libtmux_erlang"}} ]}. ``` Commit `rebar.lock` to keep the resolved commit. The [installation guide](docs/installation.md) covers application startup and building a consumer. No Hex release is advertised. ## Create, capture and query From this checkout, compile with the pinned tools: ```console $ mise exec -- rebar3 compile ``` Run the complete program below on a private tmux server: ```console $ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript readme ``` The program starts an empty daemon on a unique private socket, verifies its assertions, and retires the owned server and clients. It leaves your existing tmux sessions alone. It uses only public core APIs and OTP runtime libraries; the archive check also runs it outside this checkout. Save it as `readme_demo.erl` when reusing it in an application. ```erlang -module(readme_demo). -moduledoc "Create a workspace, query its graph and preserve captured values.". -export([run/1]). -import_record(tmux_model, [pane]). -spec run(binary()) -> map(). run(Executable) -> Options = #{executable => Executable}, {ok, Result} = tmux_server:with_owned(Options, fun(Server) -> {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server, #{name => <<"workspace">>, window_name => <<"editor">>, width => 120, height => 30, launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}), {ok, Worker} = tmux_window:create(Session, #{name => <<"workers">>, launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}), {ok, Right} = tmux_pane:split(Worker, #{direction => horizontal, launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}), {ok, _} = tmux_window:select_layout(Worker, even_horizontal), {ok, _} = tmux_pane:resize(Right, #{width => 40}), {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server), Windows = tmux_select:windows(Snapshot), Workers = #{name => <<"workers">>, panes => #{count => 2, every => #{current_command => <<"cat">>}}}, {ok, Captured} = tmux_select:one(Workers, Windows), {ok, Children} = tmux_snapshot:related(panes, Captured, Snapshot), Ids = [Id || #pane{id = Id} <:- Children], 2 = length(Ids), Criteria = #{width => #{gte => 20}, window => #{is => #{name => <<"workers">>}}}, Query = tmux_query:where(Criteria, tmux_query:panes(Server)), {ok, Fetched} = tmux_query:fetch(Query), 2 = tmux_select:size(Fetched), {ok, _} = tmux_window:rename(Worker, <<"finished">>), <<"workers">> = tmux_model:get(name, Captured), {ok, Fresh} = tmux_query:fetch(tmux_query:where( #{name => <<"finished">>}, tmux_query:windows(Server))), {ok, Renamed} = tmux_select:one(Fresh), <<"finished">> = tmux_model:get(name, Renamed), 1 = length(tmux_snapshot:sessions(Snapshot)), 2 = length(tmux_snapshot:windows(Snapshot)), 3 = length(tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot)), #{sessions => 1, windows => 2, panes => 3, matched_panes => 2, captured_name => <<"workers">>, immutable => true} end), Result. ``` The result includes this checked output. Captured rows keep their original values after a rename; actions and `fetch` perform explicit I/O. `tmux_server:with_owned/2` returns success after verified daemon cleanup. If cleanup fails, its error preserves the callback outcome and ownership token for recovery. ```json { "sessions": 1, "windows": 2, "panes": 3, "matched_panes": 2, "captured_name": "workers", "immutable": true } ``` ## Follow the graph A window can have several links in one session and belong to more than one session. Physical windows and panes remain unique; window links retain each session/index membership. - [Linked windows and relationship queries](docs/graph.md): build two sessions, link a shared window twice, and verify physical and membership counts. - [Daemon ownership](docs/ownership.md): choose private startup or a borrowed socket, keep their lifetimes explicit and handle incomplete cleanup. - [Build command values](docs/commands.md): prepare a rename and resize, submit them explicitly and inspect fresh state without changing captured rows. - [Control attachments](docs/control.md): verify connection identity, inspect attachment effects and retire the client explicitly. - [Load a workspace file](docs/workspaces.md): validate desired sessions, windows and panes, resolve working directories and inspect stable keys. - [Run a job and capture its result](docs/jobs.md): wait for a pane's completion event, check its exit status, capture bytes, and cancel a separate operation. - [Local filters and source queries](docs/querying.md): Boolean criteria, quantifiers, portable JSON, cardinality, coverage and execution plans. - [Fields and operators](docs/fields.md): generated from the runtime schema. - [Scoped options](docs/options.md): local ownership markers, explicit inheritance and sparse arrays, with a source-pinned option catalogue. - [Buffers and paste](docs/buffers.md): preserve binary artifacts, inspect names and control terminal delivery. - [Rearrange panes](docs/panes.md): isolate a running job in a window and join it back, preserving its process and the original snapshot. - [Apply configuration and await a signal](docs/configuration.md): load settings from stdin, observe the event and verify parse-only behavior. - [Pipe terminal output](docs/pipe.md): save a job's bytes, await its consumer acknowledgement and verify the resulting log. - [Hooks and completion](docs/hooks.md): register a split callback, await its acknowledgement and remove the local hook. - [Key tables](docs/keys.md): register application bindings, inspect native listings and remove the owned table. - [Native commands](docs/commands-reference.md): source-derived parser metadata and feature minimums, separate from library API and runtime qualification. - [API browser and source docs](docs/api.md): build searchable native reference pages with specs, types and links to the exact source revision. ## Decide whether it fits The current path uses bounded one-shot tmux clients. Operations support non-blocking submission, explicit waits, cancellation and ownership transfer. An await timeout abandons that wait; it does not cancel the operation. Cancellation after dispatch can leave the tmux outcome unknown. An explicit control attachment verifies identity on its persistent connection and owns its client cleanup. Control command submission, output streams and the workspace CLI remain implementation work. The [support and gaps](docs/compatibility.md) page lists what is exercised, what remains open, and the required Linux/tmux matrix. There is no control-versus-streaming performance claim. The [project policy](docs/project-policy.md) keeps core and workspace in separate OTP applications with OTP runtime dependencies. MCP is excluded from this port's scope. ## Verify and contribute ```console $ time python3 tools/check.py mid ``` ```console $ time python3 tools/check.py outer ``` The outer check owns its tmux fixtures and tests installed consumers. See [contributor setup](.github/CONTRIBUTING.md) for prerequisites and test budgets, [CI](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/actions/workflows/ci.yml) for individual release/architecture results, and the [MIT license](LICENSE). [Branding assets](docs/branding.md) include the logo, icons, and social cards.

# Install the core application

The core OTP application is `libtmux_erlang`. It lives in an umbrella, so a
Rebar3 source dependency must use `git_subdir` with `apps/libtmux_erlang`.
Using the repository root as an ordinary single-app Git dependency does not
select the core application.

The [README](../README.md#install) contains the dependency declaration tested
in an isolated Rebar3 consumer. Rebar3 resolves the branch to a commit in
`rebar.lock`; commit that file. To choose a reviewed commit directly, use
Rebar3's `{ref, Commit}` form instead of `{branch, "master"}`.

Add `libtmux_erlang` to your application's `applications` list in its
`.app.src`. For an interactive consumer, compile and start the Rebar3 shell:

```console
$ rebar3 compile
```

```console
$ rebar3 shell
```

## Inspect an existing server

`open/1` borrows an existing daemon. It does not start tmux or create a session.
From a shell attached to the server you intend to inspect, obtain its socket:

```console
$ export LIBTMUX_SOCKET="$(tmux display-message -p '#{socket_path}')"
```

Save this module as `src/inspect_demo.erl` in the consumer application:

<!-- example: examples/inspect_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(inspect_demo).
-moduledoc "Inspect an existing tmux socket without changing its sessions.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    {ok, _} = application:ensure_all_started(libtmux_erlang),
    Endpoint = #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable},
    {ok, Result} = tmux_server:with_server(Endpoint, fun(Server) ->
        {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
        #{sessions => length(tmux_snapshot:sessions(Snapshot)),
          windows => length(tmux_snapshot:windows(Snapshot)),
          panes => length(tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot))}
    end),
    Result.
```

Run it through the consumer's Rebar shell. The executable path comes from PATH;
the socket must be the absolute path selected above:

```console
$ rebar3 shell \
    --eval '
        Socket = list_to_binary(os:getenv("LIBTMUX_SOCKET")),
        Tmux = list_to_binary(os:find_executable("tmux")),
        io:format("~p~n", [inspect_demo:run(Socket, Tmux)]),
        halt().'
```

The returned map counts physical objects in one captured view. Closing the
library handle preserves the borrowed daemon and its sessions. This module
also runs against the installed archive in the outer check. The private-server
[README program](../README.md#create-capture-and-query) adds creation, native
record patterns, graph traversal and a fresh query.

Direct native-record construction needs `tmux_model` loaded first; its
constructors load normally and validate observations. Do not distribute record
headers or serialize record internals as a wire format.

## Requirements

| Component | Current requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Erlang/OTP | Exactly the qualified latest-stable baseline, 29.1.2 |
| Build tool | Rebar3 3.28.0 |
| tmux | 3.3a–3.8, including intermediate releases; CI tests both endpoints |
| Runtime platform | Linux x86_64 and arm64 qualification cells |
| Native build | C11 compiler, libc headers and make |
| Core dependencies | OTP kernel, stdlib and crypto; no JSON package or NIF |
| Checkout example runner | Python 3.12+ for owned-server readiness observation |

The helper builds from its packaged C source. Installation must fail if that
build fails; there is no runtime executable download. The helper's original
license is retained separately from the project's MIT license.

There is no published Hex package or release artifact for this checkout.
[API docs](api.md) describe the local browser build. [Compatibility](compatibility.md)
separates current checks from the remaining suite and delivery gates.

# Query a shared window without losing its memberships

This program creates two sessions, a shared two-pane window, and two extra
window links. It then checks the physical object graph and session-relative
membership counts. `tmux_window_link` acts on a session/index membership and
checks its expected physical window before dispatch.

Selecting a window membership changes that session's current window.
`tmux_session:select/2` switches one explicitly named attached client to a
session. It never attaches a client or chooses a current client implicitly.
Its `tmux_session:select/3` variant updates the destination environment only
when requested. Client names can be reused after disconnection; this call
does not provide an atomic client-incarnation check. The native API contract
documents name lookup and environment-removal semantics.

Run it on a private server after compiling:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript graph
```

<!-- example: examples/linked_graph.erl -->

```erlang
-module(linked_graph).
-moduledoc "Distinguish physical windows from their session memberships.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    Endpoint = #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable},
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(Endpoint),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        {ok, Work} = tmux_session:create(Server,
            #{name => <<"work">>, launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            {ok, Mirror} = tmux_session:create(Server,
                #{name => <<"mirror">>, launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
            tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                {ok, Shared} = tmux_window:create(Work,
                    #{name => <<"shared">>,
                      launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
                Launch = #{launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}},
                {ok, _} = tmux_pane:split(Shared, Launch),
                WorkId = tmux_model:get(id, Work),
                WindowId = tmux_model:get(id, Shared),
                {ok, Before} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
                {ok, Source} = tmux_select:one(#{window_id => WindowId},
                    tmux_select:window_links(Before)),
                {ok, _} = tmux_window_link:link(Source, Work, #{index => 7}),
                {ok, _} = tmux_window_link:link(
                    Source, Mirror, #{index => 9}),
                {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
                3 = length(tmux_snapshot:windows(Snapshot)),
                4 = length(tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot)),
                5 = length(tmux_snapshot:window_links(Snapshot)),
                {ok, CapturedWork} = tmux_snapshot:get(
                    session, WorkId, Snapshot),
                {ok, Physical} = tmux_snapshot:related(
                    windows, CapturedWork, Snapshot),
                {ok, Memberships} = tmux_snapshot:related(
                    window_links, CapturedWork, Snapshot),
                2 = length(Physical),
                3 = length(Memberships),
                Criteria = #{window_links => #{count => 3},
                    panes => #{every => #{current_command => <<"cat">>},
                        count => 2}},
                {ok, Only} = tmux_select:one(
                    Criteria, tmux_select:windows(Snapshot)),
                WindowId = tmux_model:get(id, Only),
                #{physical_windows => 3, physical_panes => 4, window_links => 5,
                  work_windows => 2, work_memberships => 3,
                  shared_window_panes => 2}
            end, fun() ->
                {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Mirror),
                ok
            end)
        end, fun() ->
            {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Work),
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).
```

There are three physical windows and four physical panes. Five window links
remain because the shared window occurs at two indexes in `work` and once
in `mirror`. `Session.windows` projects two unique windows for `work`;
`Session.window_links` retains its three memberships.

A link is identified within a capture by session, index and expected physical
window. It has no stable tmux link ID. Captured index references cannot promise
atomic compare-and-act after another client moves a link.

Use `tmux_window_link:get/3` for a fresh membership. `link/3` adds a membership;
`move/3` moves just the checked membership; `swap/3` exchanges two memberships'
physical windows. Their input rows must share one registered owner. Actions
return command results and leave captured values unchanged.

`select/1` selects the checked window in its session. `unlink/2` removes one
membership, retaining tmux's last-link protection by default. Explicit
`force => true` can destroy the physical window if its final membership goes.
`tmux_window:kill/1` destroys that window across all links.

If a captured index disappears or names another physical window, actions
return `stale_link` before dispatch. `tmux_server:bind/2` applies this same
precondition when rebinding a link to an owner. It does not adopt the new
occupant of an old index. The one-shot preflight and action are separate;
another client can still change that membership between them.

The relation query checks the full captured graph. Filtering a window selection
does not replace its panes with only matching panes. `some`, `every`, `none`
and `count` require complete membership coverage, including empty selections.
The [query guide](querying.md) explains validation and correlation.

# Capture locally; fetch explicitly

A snapshot is observed data. A selection is ordered rows plus their captured
context. A filter is portable predicate data. A query describes a future tmux
observation. Only `fetch` executes a query.

The [README program](../examples/readme_demo.erl) shows both paths against
real tmux. It retains a captured name after renaming the live window, then
executes a fresh source query. All ordinary snapshot and selection reads stay
local, even after the endpoint closes.

## Criteria

Local criteria use atom-keyed maps and binary text. Bare scalars mean equality;
fields and operators in one map conjoin. Boolean branches use quoted `'and'`,
`'or'` and `'not'`. Empty AND is true and empty OR is false. Callbacks belong
to `tmux_select:filter/2` and must return Booleans; callback failures propagate.

Relations use `some/every/none/count` for to-many values and `is/is_not` for
to-one values. One `some` containing two conditions requires the same related
row. Two separate `some` conditions can match different rows. Empty to-many
relations make `some` false and `every` and `none` true.

[Fields and operators](fields.md) come from the runtime validator. Unknown
fields, invalid operations, type mismatches and incomplete coverage fail before
row traversal. An unloaded relationship never becomes an empty relationship.
`from_list` keeps supplied order and duplicates but cannot infer relationships.

## Cardinality

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `first` | `{ok, Row}` or `none`; more matches are allowed |
| `one` | `{ok, Row}`, `{error, no_match}`, or a multiple-match error |
| `one_or_none` | `{ok, Row}`, `{ok, none}`, or a multiple-match error |
| `one_or_error` | Row directly; raises on zero or multiple matches |
| `size` | Cached materialized size |
| `count` | Current size, or exact count after supplied criteria |

Criteria come first and the selection last. Ambiguity stops after the second
match once validation is complete. `to_list/1` and `fold/3` keep ordinary Erlang
list consumers available; a selection is not a list protocol.

## Portable input

`tmux_filter:decode_json/1` rejects duplicate keys, trailing input and excessive
size/depth. `from_wire/2` maps generated wire names explicitly; it never creates
atoms from payload keys. `to_wire/1` exports filter data, not closures or native
record internals. Integral numbers normalize only within the exact shared JSON
integer range. Text is case-sensitive and is not implicitly normalized.

Run this complete local recipe. It uses captured rows and needs no tmux server:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript filter
```

<!-- example: examples/filter_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(filter_demo).
-moduledoc "Validate portable JSON and filter captured rows without tmux I/O.".
-export([run/0]).

-spec run() -> map().
run() ->
    {ok, Editor} = tmux_model:pane(#{id => <<"%1">>, active => true,
        width => 120, current_command => <<"nvim">>}),
    {ok, Shell} = tmux_model:pane(#{id => <<"%2">>, active => false,
        width => 80, current_command => <<"bash">>}),
    Panes = tmux_select:from_list(pane, [Editor, Shell]),
    Criteria = #{active => true, 'or' => [
        #{current_command => #{in => [<<"nvim">>, <<"vim">>]}},
        #{width => #{gte => 160}}
    ]},
    {ok, Filter} = tmux_filter:new(pane, Criteria),
    Encoded = iolist_to_binary(json:encode(tmux_filter:to_wire(Filter))),
    {ok, Document} = tmux_filter:decode_json(Encoded),
    {ok, RoundTrip} = tmux_filter:from_wire(pane, Document),
    {ok, Editor} = tmux_select:one(RoundTrip, Panes),
    [Editor] = tmux_select:to_list(tmux_select:where(Filter, Panes)),
    {error, #{code := duplicate_key}} = tmux_filter:decode_json(
        <<"{\"version\":1,\"version\":2}">>),
    Invalid = #{active => #{contains => <<"yes">>}},
    try tmux_select:where(Invalid, Panes) of
        _ -> error(expected_validation_error)
    catch
        error:{bad_filter, #{code := unsupported_operator} = Detail}:Stack ->
            [active, contains] = maps:get(path, Detail),
            Reason = {bad_filter, Detail},
            Message = erl_error:format_exception(error, Reason, Stack),
            Text = unicode:characters_to_binary(Message),
            {_, _} = binary:match(Text, <<"Allowed:">>)
    end,
    #{matched_ids => [tmux_model:get(id, Editor)],
      wire_round_trip => true, duplicate_keys_rejected => true}.
```

It selects `%1`, preserves the meaning of the JSON round trip, and rejects
ambiguous duplicate keys. The installed-archive check runs the same program.

The [restricted ASCII regex guide](../tools/regex-conformance/README.md) gives
its grammar and resource limits. Non-ASCII subjects and exhausted match limits
are errors, not nonmatches. Local callbacks provide other regex semantics.

## Source plans

Queries filter the complete captured graph locally by default. Enable native
candidate exclusion explicitly with `tmux_query:pushdown(true, Query)`. It can add
a candidate scan and an earlier observation without reducing graph hydration.
`tmux_query:explain/1` reports the choice in its `pushdown` field.

`tmux_query:explain/1` performs no I/O. It reports command templates, native
candidate conditions, full residual data, complete hydration, required fields,
ordering, identity policy and temporal assumptions. ID, Boolean and qualified
unsigned numeric conditions can reach tmux's `-f`. Text, nullable fields and
relations remain local. Numeric comparisons use tmux arithmetic formats,
not string ordering.

Hydration defaults to one framed list scan per nonempty entity collection.
Each field is expanded once and escaped before row/column framing, preserving
paths containing tabs, newlines and non-UTF-8 bytes. A successful nonempty
capture uses nine logical commands, plus an optional candidate scan. Identity
preflights add one tmux client per command. Linked memberships can increase
the bytes returned even though physical rows remain unique.

Each command remains bounded to 1 MiB of stdout. If a whole entity exceeds
that bound, use `hydration => isolated` in snapshot or fetch options to read
one field per physical row. The total capture bound and deadline still apply.
`commands.hydration` describes the default templates;
`commands.isolated_hydration` describes isolated reads and unqualified-schema
fallback. Snapshot metadata records the chosen strategy and actual calls.
[ADR 0002](adr-0002-batched-hydration.md) records the framing, measurements and
tradeoffs.

A candidate is a necessary condition: it can admit extra rows but must not
exclude a same-state full-filter match. Unsupported leaves become true;
AND and OR compose conservatively; NOT translates only exact children.
Membership trees are balanced to respect tmux's recursion limit.

Fetch retains a complete captured graph, validates any candidate scalar agreement,
evaluates the full local filter, and only then applies limits. Physical entities
deduplicate by ID; window links retain membership identity. `pushdown(false, Q)`
disables earlier candidate exclusion. Capture options bound rows, output and
time; `retry => 1` requests at most one inconsistent-capture retry within the
original capture deadline. The default is no retry.

Captures span several commands and are not atomic. Local re-evaluation cannot
recover rows excluded before their state changed. Atomic consistency and a
same-connection identity promise remain unsupported by this one-shot path.

# Own a daemon or borrow an endpoint

Use `tmux_server:with_owned/2` for work inside a new private daemon and
`tmux_server:with_server/2` for a callback using an existing socket. Use
`tmux_server:start_owned/1` and `tmux_server:open/1` when your application
manages those lifetimes explicitly. The
[README program](../README.md#create-capture-and-query) uses public owned
startup, graph queries and cleanup; it also runs against the installed archive.

Owned startup returns an endpoint and an ownership token. The daemon starts
empty, without a user config, in a fresh private directory. It disables
`exit-empty` on that daemon and keeps one unattached bootstrap client alive.
It does not create a session, attach an observer or change a borrowed daemon's
policy. The startup budget includes readiness, a no-start socket identity
probe and binding the endpoint to the observed Linux process incarnation.
These observations do not make connection replacement atomic.

`tmux_server:close/1` retires endpoint operations and one-shot clients without
issuing daemon destruction commands. Native policies and hooks may still
change state. Separate [control attachments](control.md) receive an
invalidation notice and begin their own retirement; close them before their
endpoint to verify their cleanup too. Closing a row's endpoint never conveys the
separate ownership token. `tmux_server:stop_owned/1` requires that token and
retires the owned endpoint, bootstrap client, daemon and finite descendants.
It targets the helper's owned process tree, never a daemon discovered by path.
The process that called startup owns this lifetime; its death also starts
cleanup. A successful stop remains idempotent for 60 seconds.

## Preserve work and cleanup failures

Scoped server callbacks run in the calling process. Successful cleanup returns
`{ok, Value}` or re-raises the callback's original error, throw or exit with its
stack. A callback returning `{error, Detail}` returns that ordinary value inside
`{ok, Value}`; the scope does not interpret application-specific results.

If cleanup fails, the result is `{error, Failure}` with
`t:tmux_server:scope_failure/0`. Its `primary` field retains the callback value
or exception, and `cleanup` retains the separate cleanup error or exception.
The failure includes `server` and, for an owned scope, `ownership`. Retain these
handles for inspection and an explicit cleanup retry. A cleanup timeout leaves
the existing supervised owner responsible; it does not establish retirement.

For nested resources, `tmux_scope:run/2` preserves the same evidence without
acquiring a resource. `tmux_scope:run_or_error/2` returns the callback value
directly and raises `{scope_cleanup_failed, Failure}` on cleanup failure.
The examples use this raising form so an inner failure propagates while outer
cleanup still runs. Each cleanup closure normalizes its resource's successful
reply to `ok`. Nested cleanup failures retain their separate evidence.

These helpers attempt cleanup once. They do not impose callback duration
limits, retry work or retire separately allocated resources automatically.
Close a control attachment explicitly before leaving its endpoint scope.

## Handle incomplete cleanup

A cleanup deadline is an error, not retirement proof. While the application
runs, the supervised controller retains uncertainty and continues receiving
retirement events. Errors include separate process, endpoint, probe and
namespace results. Incomplete startup also returns the ownership token and
captured resources for inspection and a later stop attempt.

The controller checks directory and socket filesystem identities before
removal. It preserves a changed namespace and unexpected files. It never
recursively removes the directory. A replacement socket can therefore remain
live after the original daemon retires. A later stop can retry after the
application repairs its own namespace. Filesystem checks remain observations;
they do not reserve paths against concurrent changes by trusted local code.

Stop explicitly before application shutdown when the caller needs a verified
result. The application prepares owned cleanup while its supervisors are still
running. If cleanup remains incomplete, it logs a diagnostic and writes a
private recovery report outside the socket directory, or reports the write
failure. The report records captured identities and remaining resources; it
never authorizes signalling a PID or deleting a path. No automatic recovery
runs. Stopping the OTP application itself does not establish native cleanup,
and old ownership tokens expire with that application lifetime.

See [jobs and operations](jobs.md) for per-command ownership, cancellation and
uncertain remote effects, and [support and gaps](compatibility.md) for the
separate control and streaming qualification work.

# Observe transport, operations and captures

The core emits structured OTP Logger reports under the `[libtmux]` domain.
It adds no handler, telemetry dependency or background logging process.
Your application's Logger configuration controls delivery and cost.

Enable debug reports with `logger:set_module_level(tmux_log, debug)`. Restore
the inherited level with `logger:unset_module_level(tmux_log)`, or restore the
specific override returned by `logger:get_module_level/1`. A handler must
also admit debug events. Filter its metadata by the `[libtmux]` domain prefix
or one of its child domains. These are standard
[OTP Logger configuration](https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/kernel/logger_chapter.html#configuration)
operations; they affect the Erlang node.

The implementation checks the configured module level before constructing a
report. Ordinary completion and credit reports use debug. Helper setup
failures, incomplete cleanup and owned-daemon failures use warning. An
application-shutdown cleanup summary uses error. Use
`logger:set_module_level(tmux_log, none)` to suppress these reports together.
Reports preserve the recorded outcome and cleanup evidence. Emitting them can
increase latency and consume command-deadline or caller-wait budgets.

## Report fields

`[libtmux, transport]` reports `transport_result` after a client result becomes
available. `transport` is the client's reference ID. Fields include `result`,
`code`, `outcome`, `cleanup`, `mode`, `duration_us`, `stdout_bytes`,
`stderr_bytes` and `stdin_delivered`. Duration starts when the transport owner
initializes, including native setup and retirement. A successful transport
result can contain a nonzero client exit status; the endpoint determines the
tmux operation's outcome. A later improvement in cleanup evidence produces
another result report with the same reference.

The same domain reports `transport_credit_held` when a channel delivers a
chunk and withdraws further read credit until acknowledgement. `stream`,
`sequence` and `held_bytes` identify that delivery. This records a flow-control
transition, not proof that a subscriber is slow. It does not claim a backlog
size inside tmux. One-shot output exhaustion instead appears as `output_limit`
in its result report. See [control attachments](control.md) for the currently
qualified control surface.

`[libtmux, operation]` reports `operation_result` with `generation` and
`operation` reference IDs. `phase`, `stage`, `outcome`, `cleanup`, `result`,
`code` and output byte counts describe the same evidence as
`tmux_operation:status/1` and `tmux_operation:await/2`. `tracked_duration_us`
starts when the endpoint begins tracking the operation; it excludes time
spent holding an unused admission lease. Incomplete cleanup may first produce
a `responded` report and later a `retired` report. Retirement does not turn an
unknown remote outcome into success. See [jobs and operations](jobs.md).

`[libtmux, query]` reports `capture_result` for an admitted snapshot or query
capture, including rejections after its endpoint context is established.
`capture` matches the successful snapshot's metadata ID; `generation` matches
the endpoint. `duration_us` covers that capture's observation interval and
validation. Success includes logical `source_calls` and `observed_bytes`.
Failure includes `code` and an atom-valued `reason` when available. Invalid
options and failures before endpoint context is available return their normal
errors without a capture report. Query retries have separate capture IDs.
These counters do not include the transport's identity preflight clients.
Snapshot metadata also records the hydration strategy. Batched hydration uses
three field scans on a nonempty graph; isolated hydration uses one command per
text/byte field per physical row. Both retain the six bracketing spine scans.
See [source plans](querying.md#source-plans) for bounds and the explicit option.

`[libtmux, ownership]` reports `owned_server_failure`,
`owned_server_cleanup_incomplete` and `owned_server_recovery_report_failed`.
`ownership` is a reference ID; `code` and an optional atom-valued `reason`
describe the failure. Retain the original API error for recovery handles and
resource evidence. The report grants no authority to stop a server.

Application shutdown reports `owned_server_shutdown_incomplete` in the same
domain with `scope => application`, `code` and `failed_owners`. The bounded
summary omits nested resource reports. Private recovery files retain the
separate cleanup evidence; see [daemon ownership](ownership.md).

## Cost and data boundaries

Reports contain a fixed set of reference IDs, atoms and integer counters.
They omit executable paths, socket paths, argv, environment values, terminal
bytes, names, filter criteria and full error maps. They are observations,
not durable audit records or a replacement for returned errors. Reference
IDs identify this VM's lifetimes; they are not persistent resource identities.

Caller-installed Logger metadata, filters and handlers remain under application
control. Handler callbacks run in the emitting process. Custom handlers can
delay it, and standard handlers can switch to synchronous backpressure under
load. Configure handler levels and overload protection for production.
Enabling debug on a large capture produces a report per transport and
operation. Reports describe the implemented one-shot and attachment lanes;
they do not qualify deferred command submission or public streams.

The Common Test diagnostics suite installs an owned Logger handler, exercises
real helper and tmux operations, and checks reference correlation, capture
rejection, read-credit withholding, setup failure, cleanup failure, bounded
reports, payload exclusion and disabled logging.

## Local programming errors

Library-raised validation, coverage, cardinality and explicit raising-helper
exceptions carry native EEP-54 metadata. `m:tmux_error` adds explanations to
the shell and `erl_error:format_exception/3`, including the input path,
allowed names or missing observations when available. Exception reasons and
tagged result APIs keep their structured data. Application callback exceptions
retain their original stack; the library does not relabel them as filter
failures. This formatting performs no I/O and is separate from Logger reports.

The [local filter program](querying.md#portable-input) checks a malformed
criterion and formats its native exception through the installed package.

# ADR 0001: Immutable values and owned tmux execution

## Status

Accepted architecture, 2026-11-08. Implementation and delivery remain partial.

This record describes the design selected for the
[recorded source baseline](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/tree/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b). It does not qualify unfinished APIs or
announce a release. [Support and gaps](compatibility.md) owns the current
implementation and platform inventory. A later decision that changes these
boundaries should identify which part of this record it supersedes.

[ADR 0002](adr-0002-batched-hydration.md) supersedes AD-4's field hydration
strategy with escaped entity scans and an explicit isolated option.

Upstream code references use release tags. This repository has no release tag
at this baseline; implementation links pin the recorded source commit. The
decisions below distinguish that implementation from required follow-up work.

## Context

tmux owns mutable sessions, physical windows, membership links and panes in a
separate server. Several sessions can link the same window, and one session
can contain several links to it. tmux's [pane-list traversal](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3/cmd-list-panes.c#L70-L84)
walks those links. Treating a window as a session-owned object would lose that
structure and could count one physical pane several times.

Observing the graph, acting on it and managing a client process have different
lifetimes. A captured pane can disappear before an action. A timed-out waiter
can leave a command running. A client can retire after tmux has already made
an irreversible change. The API must preserve those distinctions while fitting
ordinary Erlang programs.

The core targets the single current stable OTP baseline and tmux 3.3a–3.8 on
Linux, including intermediate releases. It does not carry older-OTP
compatibility branches. The [project policy](project-policy.md) defines the
runtime dependency and application boundaries.

## Decision drivers

- Preserve tmux identity, linked-window membership and observed coverage.
- Give callers predictable errors, ownership and cleanup evidence.
- Bound native I/O, queued operations and retained results.
- Make source-call cost and observation intervals inspectable.
- Keep ordinary Erlang use concise and downstream installation reproducible.
- Review public record compatibility independently from OTP upgrades.

## Architectural decisions

### AD-1: Use native Erlang values and explicit module functions

Use exported OTP native records for session, window, window-link and pane rows.
Keep selections, queries, filters and operation handles opaque. Criteria and
options use maps; text and terminal bytes use binaries; ordinary lists remain
the exchange format for collections.

[Native records in OTP 29](https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.1.2/system/doc/reference_manual/ref_man_native_records.md#L31) provide module-owned definitions and
record export/import without distributing a header. Their experimental status
is an explicit dependency: assess record construction, consumers and upgrades
before accepting another OTP line. Do not serialize record internals as a
public format. [Constructors](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_model.erl#L100) and action boundaries validate values;
typespecs and nominal IDs assist tooling without enforcing runtime invariants.

Exported record definitions are a versioned library contract. A value retains
the definition used when it was constructed; adding a field does not add that
field to retained values. Each release must state whether older rows and
snapshots remain usable, require conversion, or must be discarded and freshly
observed. Field renames, defaults and model-version changes need the same
review. A documented consumer restart is an acceptable initial upgrade policy.
Experimental status permits future incompatibilities; it does not establish
that every future OTP release or code upgrade will break these values.

Use [to_list/1](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_select.erl#L159) and [fold/3](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_select.erl#L165) at library boundaries.
The opaque selection itself is not an Erlang list. Arbitrary transformations
return ordinary values rather than preserving an entity selection after its
rows have changed type.

Keeping a selection retains its snapshot context. Store the extracted rows
when relationship evaluation is finished. A future compact selection must
declare its retained relationship closure and coverage; dropping related rows
cannot turn an incomplete relation into an empty complete one. Measure that
need before adding another extraction alias or pruning API.

Companion APIs provide behavioral references, with their own language
interfaces: Python's [QueryList](https://github.com/tmux-python/libtmux/blob/v0.62.0/src/libtmux/_internal/query_list.py#L327) extends a list, Elixir's
[Selection](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-elixir/blob/v0.1.1/lib/libtmux/selection.ex#L1-L13) implements Enumerable, and the OCaml core
[Map.S interface](https://github.com/ocaml/ocaml/blob/5.5.2/stdlib/map.mli#L65) describes an abstract container. Erlang uses
module functions and pattern matching. None of those companion runtimes is a
core dependency.

### AD-2: Separate physical identity, membership and observation

[tmux_model](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_model.erl#L4) distinguishes Session, Window, WindowLink and Pane.
A physical window has no universal session or session-relative index.
A window link records the observed session, index and expected physical
window; it is not a stable tmux link ID. Session window traversal deduplicates
physical windows while preserving every membership in window-link traversal.

[Snapshots](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_snapshot.erl#L3) retain immutable indexes, coverage, source calls, capture
intervals and endpoint/server generation. Server-wide physical entities use
numeric ID order. Link and pane traversal use their documented observed
indexes. Filtering preserves that order instead of exposing map iteration.

Coverage distinguishes a known value, known absence, not-loaded data and an
unavailable capability. An unloaded relationship cannot become an empty list.
[require/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_snapshot.erl#L187) checks the fields and relationships needed by an
evaluation, including when its selection is empty.

Constructed rows are detached. [bind/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_server.erl#L267) performs an explicit fresh
observation before registering an action-capable row. Actions validate the
registered origin, generation and expected membership. A vanished target does
not permit fallback to a positional target.

At the recorded baseline, the [origin registry](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_server.erl#L282) identifies an endpoint and
generation, while [target resolution](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_target.erl#L9) takes the ID from the supplied row.
Exported records permit construction and updates, including that ID and their
provenance fields. The origin therefore does not authenticate an unchanged
observation. The selected correction binds the captured target in a private,
unexported native record carried by the public row. Actions compare its entity,
origin, snapshot ID and target fields with the supplied row before dispatch.
Edited identities require fresh `tmux_server:bind/2` observation. The private
value retains identifiers rather than a graph or a per-row registry entry.
Edited-row regressions cover IDs, origins, snapshot IDs and link memberships.
The [model upgrade policy](compatibility.md#retained-rows-and-upgrades) requires
discarding version-1 values when adopting this model version 2 representation.
These checks provide library provenance, not authorization against trusted
code in the Erlang VM or callers of internal construction functions.

### AD-3: Keep selections, portable filters and source queries distinct

| Value | Meaning | Execution boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Selection | Ordered rows from one captured graph | Local reads and transformations |
| Filter | Validated, versioned predicate data | Preparation against explicit snapshot coverage |
| Query | A future source observation and its plan | Explicit fetch |

[where/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_select.erl#L107) accepts declarative criteria or a portable filter.
[filter/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_select.erl#L132) accepts a unary Boolean function; callback failures
propagate. A trusted matcher behaviour prepares local executable code. A
serialized filter cannot select a module or carry a closure.

Criteria use one map grammar with field-specific operators, Boolean
composition and explicit relationship quantifiers. A single existential child
must satisfy all conditions inside that child. Separate existential clauses
may match different children and must not be merged during normalization.
Complete coverage is required for relationship counts, every and none.

[Portable filters](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_filter.erl#L3) contain stable schema identifiers and normalized
values. [Prepared evaluation](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_filter.erl#L169) may cache membership sets, compiled
patterns and relation indexes, but remains bound to the captured context.
Checked cardinality distinguishes absence from ambiguity and stops after a
second match establishes the latter.

Composition should depend on the normalized expression, not the sequence of
query-builder calls. Compose validated filters internally and flatten adjacent
Boolean conjunctions before applying normalized limits. Preserve bounds during
external parsing and preserve separate existential nodes. The recorded
implementation still nests conjunctions through wire conversion; chained and
flat construction need an equivalent-semantics and resource-accounting test.

[OTP JSON](https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.1.2/lib/stdlib/src/json.erl#L880) owns parsing and encoding. The [wire boundary](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_json.erl#L5)
adds document and nesting limits, duplicate-key and trailing-input rejection,
exact-number bounds and explicit field mappings. Payload keys never create
atoms. Shared regex support uses the tested restricted dialect; full local
regex behavior belongs in trusted callbacks, without an interoperability claim.

### AD-4: Make observation and optimization explicit

[snapshot/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_server.erl#L245) and [fetch/2](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_query.erl#L212) perform source I/O.
Query construction, explanation and local selection reads do not refresh or
hydrate data implicitly.

Capture brackets hydration with identity/scalar scans and rejects detected
disagreements. It remains an interval of observations. A change followed by a
reversal can escape detection; immutable storage does not make capture atomic.
Stable IDs and observed process identity do not make later actions atomic.

The current `fetch/2` permits one opt-in inconsistent-capture retry within the
original deadline; `snapshot/2` has no retry option. Changing that default or
accepting disagreements in volatile fields changes the observation contract.
Measure churn before making that decision. `max_rows` bounds each raw scan and
the aggregate session/window/pane observations in each spine; repeated linked
memberships count before physical deduplication.

Native tmux filtering is a candidate optimization. For the same observed state,
the full predicate must imply the candidate predicate. The complete residual
still runs locally, required relationships remain complete, and limits apply
after residual filtering and identity handling. Unknown translations broaden
the candidate; negation requires an exact child translation.

Numeric formats need their own conversion and range qualification. Erlang term
ordering and tmux string comparison must not stand in for schema numeric
semantics. [explain/1](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_query.erl#L172) exposes the plan and its temporal limits.
Disabling pushdown avoids an earlier candidate exclusion, while retaining the
capture interval. Later filtering cannot recover a row excluded earlier.

#### Capture cost and optimization gate

The [capture sequence](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_observe.erl#L29) hydrates the complete graph even when a
candidate filter is present. With the recorded field schema, a successful
nonempty capture performs `6 + S + 2W + 3P + C` logical data commands: two
three-command spine scans, one text field per session, two per physical window,
three text/byte fields per physical pane, and an optional candidate scan `C` of
zero or one.
Each successful command also performs an identity preflight. Three sessions,
nine windows and 27 panes therefore require 108 logical commands and 216 tmux
client launches without a candidate scan. Startup, retries and failures are
outside this calculation; it is not a latency measurement.

Complete-graph queries default to pushdown disabled. Enabling it can reduce
local residual work, but does not reduce hydration and adds an earlier
exclusion point. `explain/1` and the query guide report this choice. Equivalent
workload measurements are required before changing the default.

Measure the Erlang/helper path on small, linked, changing and 200-pane graphs.
Record commands, client launches, elapsed distributions, bytes, retained memory,
capture failures and cleanup. Require identical successful payloads, IDs,
ordering and attribution before comparing one-shot and control timings. A
literal newline inside a line-framed control command can change the request;
a successful reply guard alone cannot validate a benchmark's work.

Compare qualified persistent control, lossless batching and an in-server
guard before changing the source strategy. tmux's [command queue](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3/cmd-queue.c#L719-L790)
can wait for external work, so chaining commands does not establish general
snapshot atomicity. [if-shell -F](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3/cmd-if-shell.c#L73-L103)
provides a candidate synchronous guard, subject to identity precision, alias,
hook, membership, parsing and concurrent-client qualification. Qualify text
framing per field and tmux version; paths cannot inherit a title codec merely
because one release sanitizes titles.

Candidate-scoped hydration is a later strategy if measurements justify its
coverage complexity. A subset of matching children must never be represented
as the complete relationship. Candidate implication tests must execute the
translated predicate through the CI endpoints, tmux 3.3a and 3.8.

### AD-5: Supervise resource owners and keep domain rows as values

The endpoint, transport and owned-daemon lifecycle require supervised
processes. Sessions, panes, snapshots and selections remain values; there is
no process for every domain row.

[start_owned/1](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_server.erl#L118) creates a private server namespace and returns
a separate ownership token. Borrowed endpoint close retires library clients
while preserving the borrowed daemon. Stopping an owned daemon requires its
ownership token and cleanup proof. No operation gains permission to stop a
default or borrowed server from a socket path alone.

The initiating process owns an [operation](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_operation.erl#L3). Ownership transfer
registers the new owner before acknowledging the old owner. Submission is
non-blocking with respect to command completion. Waiting, command deadlines,
cancellation, remote outcome and native cleanup are separate contracts.
[OTP response abandonment](https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.1.2/lib/stdlib/src/gen_server.erl#L1524) does not undo remote effects.
Cancellation after dispatch can leave the tmux outcome unknown; an uncertain
mutation must not be retried automatically.

A transfer timeout can also leave an uncertain ownership outcome: abandoning
the response does not retract the queued owner change. Callers reconcile the
current owner through [tmux_operation:status/1](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_operation.erl#L104) before relying on ownership. A delayed-endpoint
regression must cover the late transfer and owner-death ordering.

Keep an executable transition model for cancellation before dispatch, partial
writes, terminal responses and late retirement. Duplicate or stale events must
release admission once; stronger cleanup evidence cannot invent a known remote
outcome. Adopt a different OTP behaviour or supervisor layout only when it
improves these invariants or a measured bottleneck.

### AD-6: Use a separate bounded Linux helper for native I/O

The OTP transport launches the [bundled C11 helper](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_transport.erl#L324) with
spawn_executable. It sends the child's executable and argument vector through
the helper's framed protocol. The helper runs outside the VM and uses Linux
process and pipe interfaces. It is built from packaged source; there is no
runtime executable download.

The [private protocol](../apps/libtmux_erlang/c_src/README.md) separates stdout and stderr, grants output read
credits, bounds frames and queues, acknowledges input writes, and distinguishes
terminal delivery from observed helper exit. The helper owns its child tree
and retains incomplete cleanup as an explicit failure. A successful tmux
reply, pipe write or helper exit alone cannot prove every later aftereffect.

[Descendant retirement](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/c_src/owned_io.c#L291) reads `/proc/self/task/<pid>/children`; the Linux kernel
must expose that interface through [CONFIG_PROC_CHILDREN](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/proc_tid_children.5.html). A mounted procfs
alone is insufficient. The recorded helper first attempts the interface during
cleanup and ignores open failure; remaining descendants can then produce
`cleanup_incomplete`. Required follow-up is admission before child launch, with a
specific capability error and underlying OS error, plus a negative test that
proves no child started. Missing support must not silently select a weaker
cleanup contract.

The helper is reused from the [tagged Elixir source](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-elixir/blob/v0.1.1/c_src/owned_io.c#L380), with
[provenance and license records](../apps/libtmux_erlang/c_src/provenance.json). Its source identity does
not transfer Elixir runtime qualification to Erlang. Separate processes also
do not provide a sandbox: inherited authority, hostile forks, helper SIGKILL
and concurrently replaced filesystem entries retain documented limits.

Carry helper fixes with their source/protocol provenance and qualify each port
independently. Focused frame fuzzing, sanitizer checks and installed source
consumers complement lifecycle tests; matching the upstream digest is not a
substitute for them.

Executable argv, tmux command syntax, formats and explicit shell-command
arguments are separate interpreter boundaries. Avoiding an implicit host
shell does not suppress tmux aliases, hooks or terminal-program behavior.

### AD-7: Qualify persistent control separately from one-shot execution

[attach/3](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang/src/tmux_control.erl#L55) currently establishes explicit control-client lifetime
and identity on that persistent connection. Attachment changes attached_count.
The selected no-output/ignore-size and environment-update policies remain
visible. Existing hooks and destruction policies can still produce effects;
closing a client is not a rollback.

The [control guide](control.md) limits current qualification to attachment.
Command submission and groups need separate framing, ordering, eligibility,
certainty and cleanup evidence. tmux's [reply guards](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.8/control.c#L523-L543) coexist with
asynchronous notifications. Its [alias-expansion path](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3/cmd-parse.y#L744-L779) means a
canonical command name alone cannot establish what configured tmux will do.
The ambient-alias contract also applies to the existing attachment command and
its identity probe. Qualify those paths against configured aliases while
preserving borrowed-server configuration. Record the library's attached client
where possible; retain the raw attached count and hook effects. Any adjusted
view needs a separately named contract rather than silently subtracting the
observer.

Public output subscriptions and sampled observation streams are also unfinished.
The helper's internal credit protocol does not establish a public streaming
API. Any such API must define credits, gaps, acknowledgement and retirement,
and describe sampled observations without promising unobserved terminal history.

### AD-8: Keep workspace execution downstream and MCP excluded

Use a Rebar3 umbrella to develop independent OTP applications together.
libtmux_erlang owns the core; libtmux_erlang_workspace consumes its public API.
The core has no dependency on the workspace application. Each package owns
metadata, license and changelog material, and needs an installed-consumer check
outside the umbrella before independent delivery.

The [workspace loader](https://github.com/libtmux/libtmux-erlang/blob/9a1ca749f7bf6f082c910c99f961bb586781ab0b/apps/libtmux_erlang_workspace/src/tmux_workspace.erl#L71) currently validates versioned JSON into
inert desired state. Planning, apply and the CLI remain implementation work.
Endpoint names need host policy; loading shell text does not authorize its
execution. File loading and path resolution are synchronous trusted-filesystem
operations without an I/O deadline or atomic filesystem-snapshot guarantee.

Erlang runtime dependencies stay within OTP, alongside the recorded external
helper exception. Build, test and documentation dependencies have separate
roles. An additional runtime dependency needs a concrete capability requirement
and a new recorded decision. MCP packages, servers and SDK integration are
excluded by [project policy](project-policy.md); they are not pending packages.

### AD-9: Keep contracts and verification native to Erlang

Keep specs, exported type/callback documentation and module/function docs beside
their definitions. Native record exports and compiler documentation support
API browsers. [ct_doctest](https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.1.2/lib/common_test/src/ct_doctest.erl#L24) executes Erlang-shell examples;
reader programs exercise real tmux through owned fixtures and installed core
packages. Generated field/operator documentation shares the validation schema.

Keep failure examples useful when both an operation and cleanup fail: retain
both outcomes instead of masking the original exception in an `after` clause.
Validate more precise query/constructor/error specs through an external
Dialyzer consumer with deliberate entity mixups. Generated recursive filters
and linked graphs should agree with a small reference evaluator.

Use bounded [OTP Logger reports](diagnostics.md) for transport failures,
cleanup, IPC duration, capture rejection and held read credit. The implemented
one-shot and attachment lanes emit these reports; later lanes must preserve
their data and cost boundaries. Give structured programming errors
useful native error formatting. Keep payloads and environment secrets out of
ordinary diagnostics, and keep optional telemetry outside core dependencies.

EUnit, Common Test, properties, Dialyzer, documentation and installed-consumer
checks cover different contracts. Preserve failed or skipped evidence instead
of treating it as a passing subset. Exact source/tool/platform identities and
individual matrix conclusions determine qualification. Continuous CI uses the
latest stable Erlang/OTP release and the oldest supported and newest stable
tmux releases on both Linux architectures. Support includes the releases
between those endpoints; earlier results retain their recorded scope.
Test-loop durations do not establish throughput or a control-versus-streaming
performance claim.

Source installation is a separate gate from consuming a compiled `ebin`/`priv`
archive. Build the exact source package outside the umbrella without a prebuilt
helper or checkout-relative resources, on each supported architecture. This
gate remains open at the recorded baseline.

## Alternatives considered

| Alternative | Decision and consequence |
| --- | --- |
| Map-only domain rows | Native records provide named shapes and downstream patterns; maps remain appropriate for criteria and options. Runtime validation is still required. |
| A general collection or ORM framework | Keep the entity-aware operations small and exchange ordinary lists. Arbitrary transformations leave the selection type. |
| Mutable shared storage as the snapshot contract | Use immutable captured indexes. An internal cache or optional adapter must preserve observation identity and coverage. |
| Direct ports without the helper | A replacement must prove separate bounded output, input accounting and owned-tree retirement. The selected helper exposes those contracts explicitly. |
| A native extension inside the VM | Keep the transport helper outside the VM, accepting Linux build and IPC costs. |
| Transparent lazy relationship reads | Reject incomplete local coverage. Arrange hydration only during explicit source execution. |
| One application for core and consumers | Separate OTP applications preserve dependency direction and expose installed-package integration failures. |
| QLC, graph or ETS as the public predicate language | Defer adapters; portable filters remain data and local callers retain native Erlang tools. |

## Consequences

The public API follows Erlang conventions and supports local reuse without
transport calls. Captured context makes relationship filtering predictable,
but retaining a selection can retain its complete snapshot graph. Callers that
only need rows should exchange lists.

Native records require deliberate upgrade qualification. Linux helper builds
require a C11 compiler, make, libc and the documented Linux interfaces. Platform
support follows the tested matrix rather than the availability of an Erlang VM.

Resource ownership and bounded protocols make failure evidence explicit. They
do not make multi-command tmux actions transactional, turn socket access into
confinement, or bound arbitrary application callbacks. Observed identity checks
and filesystem cleanup retain concurrency races stated in their contracts.

At the recorded baseline, the core graph/query/one-shot path and control
attachment exist; workspace JSON loading exists; control submission, groups,
public streams, workspace plan/apply/CLI and complete delivery remain open.
Registry and shared-site publication require their own verified delivery steps.
Consult [support and gaps](compatibility.md) before selecting an execution lane.

## When to reconsider

Revisit the native-record choice when another OTP line changes representation,
construction or upgrade behavior. Revisit the helper boundary when another
platform or transport can prove the same bounded-I/O and retirement contracts.

Revisit observation guarantees if tmux supplies a server-side atomic capture
or compare-and-act primitive. Qualify control and streams before changing the
default execution lane; compare equal workloads, errors and cleanup outcomes.
Revisit caching or advanced query adapters when measured workloads justify
their additional state and lifecycle costs.

Record a separate consumer decision if MCP is brought back into scope or if a
new runtime dependency is proposed. Do not infer either change from artwork,
an empty package directory or an implementation plan.
