# ADR 0002: Batch complete-graph field hydration

## Status

Accepted architecture. Implementation qualification remains separate from
release and full-product adoption.

This supersedes the capture execution strategy in
[ADR 0001, AD-4](adr-0001-architecture.md#ad-4-make-observation-and-optimization-explicit).
The graph model, interval semantics, identity checks, coverage, limits and
explicit execution boundary remain the governing contracts.

## Context

The original one-shot capture reads each text or byte field separately. A
successful nonempty capture needs `6 + S + 2W + 3P + C` logical commands for
sessions, physical windows, physical panes and an optional candidate scan.
Each successful command also starts an identity-preflight client. Complete
hydration dominates the cost even when a query returns one pane.

A delimiter alone cannot frame paths containing tabs or newlines. A separate
length expression is also insufficient: tmux's
[format lookup](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3a/format.c#L3432)
invokes built-in callbacks on each lookup, and
[pane_current_path](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3a/format.c#L844)
reads an external process. Length and value could therefore describe different
observations. The field must be observed once before framing.

## Decision

Hydrate each nonempty entity collection with one bounded list command.
The schema explicitly admits each current text/byte field to
`escaped_columns_v1`. A field without that admission retains isolated reads.

Each field expansion applies three literal
[substitutions](https://github.com/tmux/tmux/blob/3.3a/format.c#L4513) to one
value: escape backslashes, then replace tabs and newlines with their textual
escapes. Only then add column tabs and row newlines. No payload is expanded
again as a format, command or shell program. List commands use ordinary
format expansion, preserving literal percent sequences.

The decoder requires the final newline, exact column counts, valid escapes
and bounded raw row counts. It reverses the selected tmux print layer before
field validation, including the older VIS and dollar encodings. Native
qualification covers every non-NUL byte, empty values and protocol-looking
text; NUL is outside tmux's string representation. Text fields retain schema
UTF-8 validation, while paths remain bytes.

Validate every hydrated identity against the initial spine. Repeated physical
rows from linked memberships must agree before deduplication. Missing or new
identities reject the capture; conflicting repeated values reject it too.
The final identity/scalar spine must still agree with the first. Multiple
commands and external process reads retain interval semantics, including the
possibility of undetected change and reversal.

Default snapshot and query hydration is `batched`. The existing options maps
also accept `hydration => isolated` for one field per physical row.
[Query plans](querying.md#source-plans) describe both command templates;
[snapshot metadata](api.md) records the requested strategy and actual calls.
There is no automatic fallback after an overflowing batch.

The current successful nonempty batched capture needs `9 + C` logical commands
and `18 + 2C` tmux clients: six spine scans, three hydration scans, and the
optional candidate scan. Empty collections skip their hydration command.
Unqualified schema fields can increase this cost through isolated fallback.
Native candidate filtering remains opt-in and still hydrates the complete
graph. Limits apply after full residual evaluation and identity handling.

## Resource tradeoffs

The command stdout bound remains 1 MiB, and the capture total remains 8 MiB by
default. A batch combines entity output under that command bound. Callers with
larger entity output can explicitly choose isolated hydration, distributing it
across commands under the same total and deadline. Output overflow remains an
explicit error with cleanup evidence; the library neither enlarges bounds nor
silently retries the observation. See the native capture options in the
[API guide](api.md).

The native limit regression uses 37 panes with 30,000-byte titles. Batched
capture returns `output_limit` with its bounded prefix and completed cleanup;
an explicitly requested isolated capture returns every full title.

Linked windows can increase raw batch output because the list traversal
repeats memberships. Row bounds count those observations before physical
deduplication. Fewer commands do not imply fewer transferred bytes.

## Qualification and measurements

The linked-graph regression first returned 21 logical commands, then returned
nine with equal row maps under both strategies. The real-path regression
retains tabs, newlines, carriage returns, format syntax, backslashes and a
non-UTF-8 byte. Native framing tests run at the CI endpoints, tmux 3.3a and
3.8; focused local probes also checked the distinct older print encodings.
Support remains continuous through the intermediate releases.

A controlled Linux x86_64 experiment used OTP 29.1.2, tmux 3.8, the real
Erlang/helper path and cooperating pane programs with per-process readiness.
Both strategies observed the same owned graph, and all successful full row
maps had equal hashes. Three repetitions alternated strategy order after one
default-deadline attempt per strategy. The figures below are capture medians;
they exclude fixture setup and are observations on that host, not latency
promises.

| Graph | Batched commands | Isolated commands | Batched median | Isolated median |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 session, 1 window, 1 pane | 9 | 12 | 0.065 s | 0.084 s |
| 1 session, 5 windows, 20 panes | 9 | 77 | 0.066 s | 0.556 s |
| 2 sessions, 9 linked windows, 27 panes | 9 | 107 | 0.072 s | 0.858 s |
| 2 sessions, 20 linked windows, 200 panes | 9 | 648 | 0.125 s | 6.772 s |

The isolated 200-pane default attempt reached its deadline. Its median uses
three successful repetitions with an explicit 60-second deadline; the other
cells each have four successful observations. All owned helpers, servers and
pane roots retired, and their namespaces were removed. The complete sweep,
including fresh source builds and fixture setup, took about 40 seconds.
These measurements qualify this one-shot strategy choice. They establish no
control-mode speedup, churn rate or general workload distribution.

## Alternatives and reconsideration

Persistent control submission remains a separate qualification task with
alias, framing, attribution and lifecycle obligations. A single command batch
does not establish a general atomic snapshot. In-server guards also retain
their identity and configuration qualification requirements.

Candidate-scoped hydration would reduce complete coverage and needs a distinct
contract before adoption. Reconsider this strategy if measured transferred
bytes, regex-substitution cost, large-field overflow or repeated memberships
outweigh the saved round trips. A future strategy must preserve the current
byte, coverage, identity and cleanup contracts or name its weaker guarantees.

# Wait for a terminal job, then capture its output

A successful send or command frame does not prove that a terminal program
processed input. This example runs an owned job that acknowledges terminal
parsing before it exits, then waits for tmux's `pane-died` event, checks the
exit status and captures the completed output.

The companion [terminal job](../examples/terminal_job.py) writes its result and
an ANSI device-status request. It exits successfully only after reading tmux's
reply. tmux generates that reply after parsing the preceding output. The job
writes no more output afterward. Python 3.12+ is an example dependency only.

`pane-died` alone is **not** a general output-drain barrier on tmux 3.3. This
protocol applies to this cooperating job; it does not establish completion for
an arbitrary program or reconstruct output that scrolled out of history.

The example changes options and a hook only on its new window. `remain-on-exit`
keeps the pane addressable; an empty exit banner preserves the first line.
The hook signals a tmux `wait-for` channel. There are no sleeps or capture
retries. Run from the checkout so the companion job can be located:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript job
```

<!-- example: examples/job_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(job_demo).
-moduledoc "Capture a job that acknowledges terminal parsing before it exits.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    Endpoint = #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable},
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(Endpoint),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server,
            #{name => <<"jobs">>, width => 120, height => 30,
              launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            {ok, Window} = tmux_window:create(Session,
                #{launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
            Target = [<<"-w">>, <<"-t">>, tmux_model:get(id, Window)],
            Deadline = #{deadline_ms => 2000},
            {ok, _} = tmux_option:set(Window, <<"remain-on-exit">>, <<"on">>),
            {ok, _} = tmux_option:set(
                Window, <<"remain-on-exit-format">>, <<>>),
            {ok, Hook} = tmux_command:raw(<<"set-hook">>,
                Target ++ [<<"pane-died">>, <<"wait-for -S job-finished">>]),
            {ok, _} = tmux_server:command(Server, Hook, #{}),
            {ok, Wait} = tmux_command:raw(<<"wait-for">>, [<<"job-finished">>]),
            {ok, Operation} = tmux_operation:start(Server, Wait, Deadline),
            {error, #{code := await_timeout}} =
                tmux_operation:await(Operation, 0),
            JobFile = filename:absname("examples/terminal_job.py"),
            Launch = #{argv => [<<"/usr/bin/python3">>,
                list_to_binary(JobFile)]},
            {ok, Job} = tmux_pane:split(Window, #{launch => #{shell => <<>>}}),
            {ok, _} = tmux_pane:respawn(Job, #{launch => Launch}),
            {ok, #{exit_status := 0, cleanup := complete}} =
                tmux_operation:await(Operation, 900),
            {ok, Completed} = tmux_pane:get(Server, tmux_model:get(id, Job)),
            true = tmux_model:get(dead, Completed),
            0 = tmux_model:get(exit_status, Completed),
            {ok, <<"build complete\n">>} = tmux_pane:capture(
                Completed, #{start => 0, 'end' => 0}),
            {ok, Never} = tmux_command:raw(
                <<"wait-for">>, [<<"not-signalled">>]),
            {ok, Cancelled} = tmux_operation:start(Server, Never, Deadline),
            {ok, _} = tmux_operation:await_started(Cancelled, 900),
            {ok, cancel_requested} = tmux_operation:cancel(Cancelled),
            {error, #{outcome := unknown, cleanup := complete}} =
                tmux_operation:await(Cancelled, 900),
            #{output => <<"build complete\n">>, job_status => 0,
              await_timeout_kept_operation => true,
              cancelled_outcome => unknown}
        end, fun() ->
            {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Session),
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).
```

The output is `build complete` followed by a newline, and the exit status is
zero. The zero-duration await proves that abandoning a wait leaves the
operation usable. The separate cancelled wait reports an unknown tmux outcome
and complete client cleanup; cancellation does not undo submitted work.

The example prepares an empty pane, then starts its job with
`tmux_pane:respawn/2`. Respawn keeps the pane ID. Its default launch mode,
`previous`, reuses tmux's saved command; this example supplies new argv instead.
Running panes require explicit `force => true`. Use a job-specific completion
condition and fresh observations to check the result.

Use an empty shell command to prepare a process-free pane with
`tmux_pane:split/2`. Session creation on every supported version, and window
creation before tmux 3.8, can finish that command immediately and remove the
new object. This example uses `/bin/cat` to keep its parent session and window
available across versions.

`await_started/2` returns lifecycle status, including when an operation already
failed or retired. Use `await/2` for its command result. Successful command
results preserve separate stdout/stderr binaries, stdin bytes delivered to the
client pipe, exit status, outcome and cleanup. Validation and wait errors can
contain only a code; do not assume every error contains output or certainty.
The native API defines `t:tmux_operation:completed/0`,
`t:tmux_operation:failure/0` and `t:tmux_operation:state/0`.

## Operation ownership

The process that starts an operation owns it. Other processes can await its
handle without becoming owners. The endpoint confirms a transfer after
monitoring the new owner and releasing the old monitor; the new process does
not perform a handshake. Owner death and cancellation retire queued or
possibly-sent clients; they do not replay mutations.

An `await_timeout` from `tmux_operation:transfer/2` leaves the transfer outcome
uncertain: the endpoint may process the owner change after the caller stops
waiting. Read `tmux_operation:status/1` to establish the current owner before
relying on ownership. The timeout does not prove the old owner still owns the
operation.

Retired results are retained for at most 60 seconds. The endpoint also evicts
the oldest results when retention exceeds 64 results or 4 MiB of stdout/stderr.
Use `tmux_operation:status/1` while a handle is valid, and handle
`operation_expired` after retention. Closing an endpoint retires its library
clients and preserves the tmux server. [Daemon ownership](ownership.md)
explains the separate token used to stop an owned daemon.

Current operations use one-shot clients. Persistent control, grouping and
stream delivery are not yet available; see [support and gaps](compatibility.md).

# Own a control attachment

Attach to an existing session, verify identity on that persistent connection,
inspect its attachment effects and close the client. This currently qualifies
connection lifetime only. Commands still execute through the one-shot APIs;
control submission and groups remain implementation work.

The example owns its session. The runner provides a private tmux fixture and
verifies final cleanup:

```console

```

-module(control_demo).
-moduledoc "Attach explicitly, inspect captured values and prove detachment.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(
        #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable}),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server,
            #{name => <<"control-demo">>, width => 120, height => 30,
              launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            Id = tmux_model:get(id, Session),
            0 = tmux_model:get(attached_count, Session),
            {ok, Control} = tmux_control:attach(Server, Session, #{}),
            tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                {ok, #{phase := open, identity := same_connection}} =
                    tmux_control:status(Control),
                {ok, Attached} = tmux_session:get(Server, Id),
                1 = tmux_model:get(attached_count, Attached),
                {ok, Graph} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
                [Window] = tmux_snapshot:windows(Graph),
                120 = tmux_model:get(width, Window),
                30 = tmux_model:get(height, Window),
                ok = tmux_control:close(Control),
                {ok, #{phase := closed, cleanup := complete}} =
                    tmux_control:status(Control),
                {ok, Detached} = tmux_session:get(Server, Id),
                0 = tmux_model:get(attached_count, Detached),
                0 = tmux_model:get(attached_count, Session),
                #{identity => same_connection, attached_count => 1,
                  detached_count => 0, window_size => [120, 30],
                  cleanup => complete, session_preserved => true}
            end, fun() ->
                ok = tmux_control:close(Control)
            end)
        end, fun() ->
            {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Session),
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).

An attachment requires a session captured or bound through the same endpoint.

closed and reports cleanup explicitly. Successfully closed handles remain
usable for status and idempotent close for 60 seconds. Application shutdown
alone does not prove cleanup.

Unexpected hook output or reply blocks reject attachment and retire the client.

            {ok, [Anchor]} = tmux_snapshot:related(panes, Window, Initial),

            Pid = tmux_model:get(pid, Isolated),
            Temporary = tmux_model:get(window_id, Isolated),
            true = Temporary =/= WindowId,

            WindowId = tmux_model:get(window_id, OldPane),

            WindowId = tmux_model:get(window_id, Joined),
            Pid = tmux_model:get(pid, Joined),

            {ok, Final} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),

              temporary_window_removed => true, panes_after_join => 2}

## Supply a membership when breaking a pane

A physical window can be linked several times, even within one session. A pane
therefore has no single source membership. `tmux_pane:break/4` takes the pane,
an explicit source window link, the destination session and placement options.
`index` is required. `detach` defaults to true; false selects the destination
membership. `name` is a literal UTF-8 argument, without format expansion.

| Source window | What tmux changes |
| --- | --- |
| Several panes | Creates a physical window and moves the pane into it; the original links remain |
| Only one pane | Moves the selected membership of the existing physical window; other links remain |

Pane IDs and running processes survive both cases. Moving the final membership
out of a session can destroy that source session. Session groups retain tmux's
native synchronization behavior. An occupied destination index is refused.

The API checks the link's expected window and the pane's observed parent. It
then sends a session/index selector qualified by the stable pane ID. An absent
pane cannot become whichever pane later occupies its old positional index.
The preflight and action remain separate commands: concurrent changes after
the check, including an index moving away and back, can remain undetected.
There is no atomic compare-and-act guarantee.

Literal means unexpanded, not stored verbatim. tmux's own name cleaning still
applies. For example, 3.3/3.4 stores an added backslash before dollar-variable
prefixes; later releases changed that behavior. The library returns the
stored name instead of guessing which escapes a caller intended. See the
[object graph guide](graph.md) for physical windows and memberships.

## Move and swap by physical pane ID

`tmux_pane:join/3` and `tmux_pane:move/3` use the source and destination pane
IDs. Their native commands share placement behavior and permit rearrangement
within one window. Geometry uses `t:tmux_pane:join_options/0`: vertical by
default, optional direction, cells/percent size, `before` and `full_size`.
Both reject identical source/destination IDs.

`tmux_pane:swap/3` exchanges layout positions within or across windows. Its
`detach` defaults to true; `zoom` maps to tmux's `-Z` retention flag. Swapping
a pane with itself exchanges nothing, but native zoom handling still runs:
the default can unzoom even that same-pane call. Across windows, active
positions can receive different pane IDs even in detached mode.

Moving the last pane out destroys its physical window and every link to it,
and can remove sessions. Shared windows affect all memberships. Existing
processes keep their process environment and working directory; inherited
window options can change when the pane changes parent. With `detach` false,
join/move selection uses tmux's resolved destination-session context. Supply
window-link actions separately when a particular session membership must be
selected.

## Keep captures and action results separate

These calls return the completed command result for both new-window and
existing-window cases. They never refresh input records or captures. Use
`tmux_pane:get/2`, `tmux_window_link:get/3` or `tmux_server:snapshot/1` to observe
the resulting graph. Source/destination rows must use the same registered
owner; rebind explicitly when working through another endpoint owner.

A disappeared pane or session remains an operational error. A replaced source
link returns `stale_link`; a different observed pane parent returns
`pane_link_mismatch`. Even an eventual native layout error can unzoom windows.
These operations are not transactions and are never automatically retried.
The [support page](compatibility.md) separates implemented APIs from remaining
control, consumer and delivery qualification.

# Preserve byte buffers and paste deliberately

Store a binary artifact without sending it through a shell, terminal renderer
or Unicode conversion. Loading uses tmux client stdin; showing a buffer reads
its exact bytes, including NUL, invalid UTF-8 and protocol-like lines.

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript buffers
```

<!-- example: examples/buffer_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(buffer_demo).
-moduledoc "Store a binary artifact without terminal or text conversion.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    Name = <<"libtmux-example-",
        (binary:encode_hex(crypto:strong_rand_bytes(8), lowercase))/binary>>,
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(
        #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable}),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            Bytes = <<0, 255, "build\n%end 1 2 3\n\\r">>,
            {ok, _} = tmux_buffer:load(Server, Name, Bytes),
            {ok, Bytes} = tmux_buffer:show(Server, Name),
            {ok, [#{name := Name, size := Size} | _]} =
                tmux_buffer:list(Server),
            Size = byte_size(Bytes),
            {ok, _} = tmux_buffer:load(Server, Name, <<>>),
            {ok, Bytes} = tmux_buffer:show(Server, Name),
            #{byte_count => Size, exact_round_trip => true,
              empty_load_kept_bytes => true}
        end, fun() ->
            case tmux_buffer:delete(Server, Name) of
                {ok, _} -> ok;
                {error, #{code := buffer_not_found}} -> ok;
                Failure -> error({buffer_cleanup_failed, Failure})
            end,
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).
```

## Choose a name or the newest buffer

`tmux_buffer:load/3` accepts a binary name or `automatic`, which lets tmux
allocate a name. `show/2`, `delete/2` and `paste/3` accept an observed binary
name or `latest`. `list/1` returns ordinary metadata maps in tmux's newest-first
insertion order, with name, size in bytes and Unix creation time. It does not
load payloads. Renaming keeps the order; loading replacement data inserts a
new buffer.

Names are NUL-free bytes. tmux 3.7+ applies its own name cleaning, which can
reject controls and escape backslashes. Subsequent calls need the actual
stored name from `list/1`. The list codec preserves embedded delimiters,
newlines and invalid UTF-8 on releases that allow those names. It never uses
a newline inside a name as a row boundary.

Empty load input is a native no-op: it neither creates a buffer nor truncates
an existing one. Delete explicitly when the buffer should disappear. A named
rename refuses an occupied destination on tmux 3.3/3.3a; 3.4+ replaces it.
Identical rename inputs fail before dispatch because some legacy versions
have unsafe handling of that case.

On 3.3/3.3a, native named delete/rename falls back to the newest buffer when
the requested name is absent. These APIs first perform a targeted existence
read with zero output allowance and return `buffer_not_found` for a missing
name. The read retains no payload and is independent of list bounds.
That preflight is not atomic:
concurrent removal after the check can still trigger the native fallback.
Serialize external changes or use tmux 3.4+ when that race is unacceptable.
Buffer names do not provide stable object identities or transactional updates.

## Paste bytes into a registered pane

`tmux_buffer:paste/3` takes a registered pane, a buffer name or `latest`, and
an options map. Defaults preserve bytes: LF separators, no sanitization, no
bracketing and no deletion. Set `separator` to replace each LF with a chosen
NUL-free byte string. It is passed literally, without format expansion.

`sanitize => true` requires tmux 3.7+; older releases return
`unsupported_capability` before dispatch. The default raw path uses `-S` on
newer releases. `bracketed => true` adds markers only when the target has
enabled bracketed paste. `delete => true` removes the buffer after the native
paste call, including cases where native input-off handling discards input.

A completed paste is a tmux command result, not proof that a child consumed
input. The integration test uses a raw terminal receiver and a separate socket
acknowledgment to verify all 256 byte values and custom separators. The
[job guide](jobs.md) explains completion signals and operation ownership.

## Bound reads and preserve errors

Load input shares the endpoint's 256 KiB command admission budget with argv.
`show/3` accepts `max_bytes` from 0 through 1 MiB and `deadline_ms` from 1 through
600000. Defaults are 1 MiB and 2500 ms. Overflow returns `output_limit` with
partial command evidence; it never returns a successful truncated buffer.
Lists are bounded to 4096 rows and 1 MiB of encoded output.

Missing buffers, gone panes and closed endpoints remain distinct errors.
Timeouts do not undo a completed load or paste, and mutations are not retried.
`tmux_buffer:capabilities/1` describes source-defined behavior without I/O;
the [support page](compatibility.md) separates that metadata from qualification.

## Select the table explicitly

| Scope argument | Table |
| --- | --- |
| Registered session record | Local session options |
| Registered physical window record | Local window options, shared by its memberships |
| Registered pane record | Local pane options |
| `{server, Server}` | Server-wide options |
| `{session_defaults, Server}` | Global session defaults |
| `{window_defaults, Server}` | Global window defaults |

A physical window has no universal parent session. Session options require a
session record; passing a pane to a session option fails rather than choosing
an incidental session. Built-in names can override tmux's native scope flags;
the wrapper checks their source metadata before dispatch to prevent that.

`get/3` uses local-only reads with `#{}`. `#{inherit => true}` follows the
selected table's parents: session defaults, or window/window defaults for a
pane. User options follow the same table ancestry. Server options have no
parent. There is no inheritance from a session table to a window table.

## Preserve absence and bytes

`none` means the selected local option or requested array entry is absent.
`{ok, <<>>}` means a known empty value. A whole array returns `{ok, Entries}`
with numeric indexes as map keys; an empty local array returns `{ok, #{}}`.
An unloaded graph field is unrelated to these live reads.

Set array entries with `{Name, Index}`. The API deliberately avoids whole-array
assignment and its separator grammar. `unset/2` removes an entry or local option;
removing a local option restores inheritance. Unsetting a global built-in resets
its tmux default. Non-numeric array keys are outside this API; an observed array
with such keys fails decoding instead of silently dropping entries.

Values are NUL-free binaries, including arbitrary bytes. Names are literal;
`#{...}` in a user-option name does not expand. Prefixes, aliases and bracket
syntax in names are rejected. A scalar value is passed without `-F`, although
tmux may interpret a stored format or executable option later. Use this API
only with trusted option names and values; it is not an external write policy.

`append` uses tmux's `-a` behavior for the selected type. `only_if_unset` uses
`-o` and reports already-set as an error. Empty flag values retain tmux's toggle
behavior; use explicit `<<"on">>` or `<<"off">>` when state must be predictable.
Mutations are not retried after a timeout or unknown outcome.

## Discover version support

The [generated catalogue](options-reference.md) lists canonical names, scopes,
parser types, arrays and hooks from pinned release commits.
`tmux_option:describe/2` and `catalogue/1` read that metadata without I/O.
Built-ins have exact source catalogues for every release from 3.3a through
3.8, including intermediate patch releases. Tracking builds and unknown
versions return `unsupported_option_catalogue`; unavailable built-ins return
`unsupported_tmux_option`. User options do not depend on a built-in catalogue.

Hooks are executable commands and are rejected by this API, including hook
names discovered in the catalogue. The [job example](jobs.md) currently uses an
explicit raw `set-hook` command. A typed hook API remains implementation work.
Raw commands are also available for deliberate newer-version integration.
A missing target remains an operational error, never a missing option.

split a pane. The hook writes a session option and signals the unique channel.
The program checks that effect, removes the local hook and verifies cleanup.

-module(hook_demo).
-moduledoc "Acknowledge a registered split hook before reading its effect.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(
        #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable}),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        Launch = #{launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}},
        {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server,
            Launch#{name => <<"hooks">>}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
            [Pane] = tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot),
            Suffix = binary:encode_hex(crypto:strong_rand_bytes(8), lowercase),
            Channel = <<"hook-", Suffix/binary>>,
            {ok, Mark} = tmux_command:raw(<<"set-option">>,
                [<<"-t">>, tmux_model:get(id, Session),
                 <<"@last-event">>, <<"split complete">>]),
            {ok, Signal} = tmux_command:wait_for(Channel, signal),
            {ok, Wait} = tmux_command:wait_for(Channel, wait),
            {ok, Operation} = tmux_operation:start(Server, Wait, #{}),
            tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                Name = <<"after-split-window">>,
                {ok, _} = tmux_hook:set(Session, {Name, 4}, [Mark, Signal]),
                {ok, _} = tmux_pane:split(Pane, Launch),
                {ok, #{cleanup := complete}} =
                    tmux_operation:await(Operation, 900),
                {ok, <<"split complete">>} =
                    tmux_option:get(Session, <<"@last-event">>, #{}),
                {ok, #{4 := _}} = tmux_hook:get(Session, Name, #{}),
                {ok, _} = tmux_hook:unset(Session, Name),
                none = tmux_hook:get(Session, Name, #{}),
                #{event => <<"split complete">>, hook_acknowledged => true,
                  local_hook_removed => true}
            end, fun() ->
                tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                    {ok, _} = tmux_operation:cancel(Operation)
                end, fun() ->
                    case tmux_operation:await(Operation, 900) of
                        {ok, #{cleanup := complete}} -> ok;
                        {error, #{cleanup := complete}} -> ok
                    end
                end), ok
            end)
        end, fun() ->
            {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Session),
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).

## Choose the table explicitly

`tmux_hook:set/3` requires a `{Name, Index}` key and validated
`tmux_command` values. It replaces that indexed entry while preserving other
entries. `append/3` chooses tmux's first vacant local index, which can precede
existing sparse entries. Commands run in index order. Bodies can be one
command or a nonempty list; rendering is bounded before dispatch.

Local tables use registered session, physical window or pane rows. Global
tables use `{session_defaults, Server}` or `{window_defaults, Server}`.
The [source catalogue](options-reference.md) defines each builtin hook's
permitted scope and version. Prefixes, aliases, ordinary options and custom
event/monitor interfaces are rejected by this API.

`get/3` reads local values by default. `inherit => true` follows parent tables.
An absent local array returns `none`; an empty array returns `{ok, #{}}` and
masks inheritance. `clear/2` leaves that empty override. `unset/2` removes an
entry or restores inheritance for the whole array. Unsetting an entry can
leave its local array empty. Global unset resets the native default.

Read values are tmux's canonical command-list text, including its own quoting
and escapes. They are not individual argument values or the original source
text. A read never executes them.

## Separate registration, context and completion

Registration confirms that tmux stored the commands. Those commands still
interpret their values and formats when they run. Native parsing can fail;
a failed first indexed write can already leave an empty local override.
There is no rollback or automatic retry of an uncertain mutation.

`tmux_hook:run/2` requests native execution in an explicit context. Use a
session for its current window/pane, a checked window link for one membership,
or `{pane, Pane, Link}` for that pane and membership. This preserves the
chosen session and index when a physical window is linked more than once. A
physical window alone cannot choose that execution context. Existence and
membership checks precede dispatch. If the target disappears after preflight,
tmux can still fall back to another context. These separate observations do
not provide atomic compare-and-act.

A native command result does not acknowledge background work launched by a
hook. The program waits for its own signal after the option write. Clearing
or unsetting a hook does not cancel effects tmux has already queued.
[Window memberships](graph.md) and [scoped options](options.md) explain the
related graph and inheritance rules.

## Registration and execution are separate

`tmux_key:bind/3` registers in the native prefix table.
`tmux_key:bind/4` accepts an explicit `table`, Boolean `repeat` and byte `note`.
It accepts one command or a flat nonempty command list, with the bounds of
`tmux_command:to_config/1`: at most 256 commands and 32 KiB of rendered text.
tmux parses the body before replacing an existing binding. Replacement resets
the previous commands, repeat flag and note.

Tables belong to the server. Creating one does not select it for any client.
Choose a session's default through the `key-table` option in
[`tmux_option`](options.md); native prefix, repeat and client table-switching
rules still apply. The example leaves client selection to the application.

Registration quotes arguments for the stored command parser. A command can
still interpret formats when a client executes it: the example's
`#{session_name}` is evaluated then. See
[configuration boundaries](configuration.md) before storing nested command
strings or explicit shell commands. An accepted registration does not prove
future execution; arrange a completion signal when an application needs one,
as in the [hook example](hooks.md).

## Read listings and remove owned bindings

`tmux_key:listing/1` and `tmux_key:listing/2` return native bytes unchanged.
Options can restrict `table` and `key`. Spacing, quoting and included metadata
follow the daemon release. This is a presentation view: retain original command
values for reinstalling bindings. tmux 3.4 may escape dollar signs in this
view. On tmux 3.7c, a single matching entry can go to the native status-message
path and produce empty stdout when no target client is attached. Empty output
does not prove a binding is absent. The example lists multiple bindings to
avoid that path. The tmux 3.3 baseline has no custom listing format option.
Explicit newer-server options remain available through
`tmux_command:raw/2`.

`tmux_key:unbind/2` and `tmux_key:unbind/3` remove one binding; an absent key in
an existing table is a native no-op. Removing the final custom binding may
remove its table.
Missing explicitly named tables and invalid native key names remain errors.
`tmux_key:clear_table/2` requires an explicit name and removes the entire
table. It can affect attached clients and does not restore default bindings
or cancel commands already queued by a client.

Calls use the registered endpoint identity and preserve backend diagnostics.
They do not start a missing server or retry uncertain mutations. The native
[`tmux_key` API browser](api.md) documents input bounds, results and errors.

        end, fun() ->

## Choose input and execution separately

`tmux_command:to_config/1` renders one validated command value or a nonempty
flat list as native configuration text. Lists contain at most 256 commands and
share the 32 KiB rendered limit, including native separators. Rendering a list
does not provide atomic execution or rollback. Argument quoting preserves
literal bytes through the lexer, including variables, semicolons, newline
indentation and non-UTF-8 byte values. It returns ASCII text without
performing I/O. Escaping growth is bounded by a 32 KiB rendered limit. This
covers one lexer pass; native commands that accept command strings can parse
those strings again. Render each inner command separately for its own
boundary. Native commands still interpret their arguments and formats
normally; this renderer does not quote shell code.

`tmux_command:source_file/2` builds a command value without I/O. The source is
`stdin` or one absolute POSIX byte path. Path glob characters and backslashes
are quoted for tmux's glob parser; hash formats are not expanded. The builder
never opens the file. Reading and parsing occur when the command executes.
The file's size is not bounded by the command builder.

For stdin, pass bytes through the execution options of
`tmux_server:command/3` or `tmux_operation:start/3`. The transport bounds stdin
and rendered arguments together to 256 KiB. `parse_only` requests native
`-n`: parse the input without executing its command list. `quiet` requests
native missing-file suppression; syntax and execution errors remain errors.
Both options default to false.

Configuration is trusted tmux code, with native directives and variable
expansion. Parse-only is not a sandbox. Execution can change state before
reporting an error, and cancellation cannot roll back those effects. A
successful source command does not establish that background work launched
by that configuration has finished. Check its actual completion event.

## Coordinate channels explicitly

`tmux_command:wait_for/2` accepts a binary channel name and one action: `wait`,
`signal`, `lock` or `unlock`. Submit its result through the same execution
APIs. Native channel names are server-wide; use a name unique to the operation
when other clients share the server.

A signal wakes current waiters. On an unlocked channel with no waiters or
pending wakeup, it retains one wakeup for a later wait. Signaling again before
a wait can clear that pending state. Send once per expected wait; repeated
signals are neither counted nor reliably coalesced. Use separate names for
signaling and locking. `lock` and `unlock` expose native advisory channel
locks. A lock remains held after the acquiring command
client exits, until an explicit unlock. They are not library-owned leases.
Cancelling a command does not undo a signal or release a possibly acquired
lock. An uncertain lock outcome requires application coordination before
unlocking; blindly unlocking can release another client's lock.

# Build commands before running them

Prepare a literal session rename and a pane resize, then submit the values
explicitly. Building validates their captured target and arguments without
contacting tmux. Execution checks the endpoint origin and returns the native
one-shot result. The resize uses an operation handle so waiting is explicit.

This complete program checks the name before execution, awaits the resize,
reads fresh dimensions and verifies that earlier rows keep their values. The
runner owns the private fixture and verifies cleanup:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript commands
```

<!-- example: examples/command_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(command_demo).
-moduledoc "Build captured-target commands, then execute and inspect them.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    Endpoint = #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable},
    {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(Endpoint),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server,
            #{name => <<"commands">>, width => 120, height => 30,
              launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            SessionId = tmux_model:get(id, Session),
            {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
            [Anchor] = tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot),
            {ok, Pane} = tmux_pane:split(Anchor,
                #{direction => horizontal, size => {cells, 40},
                  launch => #{argv => [<<"/bin/cat">>]}}),
            {ok, Rename} = tmux_session:rename_command(
                Session, <<"commands-ready">>),
            {ok, Resize} = tmux_pane:resize_command(Pane, #{width => 60}),
            {ok, OtherEndpoint} = tmux_server:open(Endpoint),
            tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                {error, #{code := different_owner, submitted := false}} =
                    tmux_server:command(OtherEndpoint, Rename, #{})
            end, fun() ->
                ok = tmux_server:close(OtherEndpoint)
            end),
            {ok, Before} = tmux_session:get(Server, SessionId),
            <<"commands">> = tmux_model:get(name, Before),
            40 = tmux_model:get(width, Pane),
            {ok, #{exit_status := 0, cleanup := complete}} =
                tmux_server:command(Server, Rename, #{}),
            {ok, Operation} = tmux_operation:start(Server, Resize, #{}),
            {ok, #{exit_status := 0, cleanup := complete}} =
                tmux_operation:await(Operation, 900),
            {ok, Current} = tmux_pane:get(Server, tmux_model:get(id, Pane)),
            60 = tmux_model:get(width, Current),
            {ok, Renamed} = tmux_session:get(Server, SessionId),
            <<"commands-ready">> = tmux_model:get(name, Renamed),
            <<"commands">> = tmux_model:get(name, Session),
            40 = tmux_model:get(width, Pane),
            #{name => <<"commands-ready">>, initial_width => 40,
              actual_width => 60, captured_values_unchanged => true,
              foreign_origin_rejected => true}
        end, fun() ->
            {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Session),
            ok
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
    end).
```

A command keeps the originating row's endpoint token. Submitting it through
another endpoint returns `different_owner` with `submitted = false`, even if
both servers happen to use the same pane or session ID. Building alone does
not establish endpoint liveness. The example rejects a second endpoint handle
to the same daemon too. To act through another endpoint, bind the row there
and build a new command. Bind detached rows with
`tmux_server:bind/2` before building their commands.

`tmux_command:to_config/1` renders command syntax without
executing it. Serialized configuration carries no origin token; the caller
must choose and validate that destination explicitly. See

# Support and remaining gaps

Support covers tmux **3.3a–3.8**, including intermediate releases, on Linux
x86_64 and arm64. The [workflow](../.github/workflows/ci.yml) tests the oldest
supported and newest stable tmux releases on both architectures.
OTP 29.1.2 is the only supported Erlang baseline;
older-OTP compatibility branches are not maintained. Native records remain an
experimental language dependency in OTP 29. Do not persist their internals or
assume compatibility with another OTP line.

| Platform | tmux releases in the required matrix |
| --- | --- |
| Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64 | 3.3a, 3.8 |
| Ubuntu 24.04 arm64 | 3.3a, 3.8 |

CI uses only the latest stable Erlang/OTP release. Testing the endpoints keeps
the routine matrix small; it does not exclude releases between them from
support. Earlier intermediate-version results retain their recorded scope.

Inspect the individual jobs at the commit you will consume. A minimum-version
check does not prove runtime support on every newer release. Tracking builds,
macOS, native Windows and psmux are not advertised as qualified platforms.

Linux must provide readable `/proc/self/task/<pid>/children`, enabled by
CONFIG_PROC_CHILDREN. The helper checks this interface before launching a
child. An unavailable interface returns `unsupported_capability` with
`capability => proc_children`, the OS `errno` and `outcome => not_started`.
See the [helper protocol](../apps/libtmux_erlang/c_src/README.md) for cleanup
evidence and the limits of native process ownership.

## Retained rows and upgrades

Native model version 2 adds a private captured target association to each
observed row. Actions check the entity, stable ID, origin and snapshot ID;
pane associations also retain the observed window and index, and window-link
associations retain their session, index and expected physical window.
Actions reject edited target fields before dispatch. Valid-shaped binding
mismatches return `observation_mismatch`; detached and malformed rows retain
their validation errors. `tmux_server:bind/2` reads the requested target and returns
a new actionable row. Ordinary record matching and detached constructors
remain available.

The private value retains identifiers, not the snapshot graph. It prevents
accidental retargeting through public row updates; it is not an authorization
boundary against trusted code running inside the VM. The internal construction
functions remain implementation details.

Discard version-1 rows and snapshots when upgrading to model version 2. Stop
consumers that retain them, clear their process/ETS state and freshly observe
the server after restart. This release supplies no `appup`/`relup` conversion.
Old or unknown model versions fail row validation. New code must validate a
retained value before accessing fields added by another model version.

Every exported-field addition, rename, removal or default change requires a
model compatibility review independently of the OTP version. Its changelog
must state whether retained values remain usable, need an explicit validated
conversion, or must be discarded. Do not assume hot loading changes fields in
existing native values.

`tmux_model:to_map/1` extracts the documented domain fields from a valid row.
Validate those fields with the destination model's constructor when migrating
data. The map loses actionable provenance; bind it through a freshly
constructed row before an action. It is not a versioned storage or cross-port
wire format: absence atoms, binary bytes and field inventories still require
an application-defined schema.

# Save a job's output and verify the consumer received it

This program opens a pane pipe before releasing the producer. A shell consumer
reads the expected bytes into a log and signals completion only after that
write succeeds. The Erlang caller verifies the file contents before stopping
the pipe. It does not infer delivery from pipe creation or command completion.

Compile the project:

```console
$ mise exec -- rebar3 compile
```

Run on an owned server. The runner verifies session and process cleanup:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript pipe
```

<!-- example: examples/pipe_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(pipe_demo).
-moduledoc "Save terminal bytes after a consumer acknowledgement.".
-export([run/2]).

-spec run(binary(), binary()) -> map().
run(Socket, Executable) ->
    Suffix = binary:encode_hex(crypto:strong_rand_bytes(8), lowercase),
    Directory = <<"/tmp/ltm-pipe-example-", Suffix/binary>>,
    ok = file:make_dir(Directory),
    tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        ok = file:change_mode(Directory, 8#700),
        Log = <<Directory/binary, "/job.log">>,
        {ok, Server} = tmux_server:open(
            #{socket_path => Socket, executable => Executable}),
        tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
            Native = <<(quote(Executable))/binary,
                " -N -S ", (quote(Socket))/binary, " wait-for ">>,
            Start = <<"start-", Suffix/binary>>,
            Done = <<"consumed-", Suffix/binary>>,
            Producer = <<"stty -onlcr && ", Native/binary, Start/binary,
                " && printf 'build complete\\n' && exec /bin/cat">>,
            {ok, Session} = tmux_session:create(Server,
                #{name => <<"pipe-example">>, launch => #{argv =>
                    [<<"/bin/sh">>, <<"-c">>, Producer]}}),
            tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
                {ok, Snapshot} = tmux_server:snapshot(Server),
                [Pane] = tmux_snapshot:panes(Snapshot),
                Payload = <<"build complete\n">>,
                Size = integer_to_binary(byte_size(Payload)),
                Consumer = <<"/usr/bin/head -c ", Size/binary,
                    " > ", (quote(Log))/binary, " && ", Native/binary,
                    "-S ", Done/binary, " && exec /bin/cat >/dev/null">>,
                {ok, Wait} = tmux_command:wait_for(Done, wait),
                {ok, Operation} = tmux_operation:start(Server, Wait, #{}),
                {ok, _} = tmux_pane:pipe(Pane, #{shell => Consumer}, #{}),
                {ok, Signal} = tmux_command:wait_for(Start, signal),
                {ok, _} = tmux_server:command(Server, Signal, #{}),
                {ok, #{cleanup := complete}} =
                    tmux_operation:await(Operation, 900),
                {ok, Payload} = file:read_file(Log),
                {ok, _} = tmux_pane:stop_pipe(Pane),
                #{log => Payload, bytes_written => byte_size(Payload),
                  consumer_acknowledged => true}
            end, fun() ->
                {ok, _} = tmux_session:kill(Session),
                ok
            end)
        end, fun() ->
            ok = tmux_server:close(Server)
        end)
    end, fun() ->
        ok = file:del_dir_r(Directory)
    end).

quote(Value) ->
    Escaped = binary:replace(Value, <<"'">>, <<"'\\''">>, [global]),
    <<"'", Escaped/binary, "'">>.
```

## Choose direction and replacement behavior

`tmux_pane:pipe/3` requires an explicit shell-command map and a registered
physical pane. It escapes hash and strftime directives before tmux expands
that text. The shell still interprets the command; the example's `quote/1`
handles values inserted into its shell code. This native operation takes shell
code rather than executable argv.

`tmux_command:literal_format/2` documents the encoding limits. Percent-bearing
commands above tmux's 8191-byte intermediate time-format limit return
`format_limit` before dispatch. That check preserves an existing pipe when a
replacement cannot be represented safely.

| Direction | Connection |
| --- | --- |
| `output` (default) | Pane PTY output to child stdin |
| `input` | Child stdout to pane input |
| `both` | Both connections |

Terminal modes affect these bytes. This is neither rendered screen capture
nor a replay of prior terminal history. It is not an Erlang subscription with
library flow control. Child stderr is discarded; unused directions use tmux's
native null-device routing. The API does not copy the pane's cwd or environment
into the child process.

Starting a pipe normally replaces an existing one. `toggle => true` maps to
native `-o`: an open pipe is closed without starting another, while a closed
pipe is opened. It does not mean preserve an already open pipe.

## Distinguish the pipe from its process

A successful action proves command completion, not shell execution success,
consumer readiness, delivered bytes or process exit. The example observes the
consumer's actual file write. Native integration tests independently verify
all 256 byte values in both directions, literal hash/percent shell text,
replacement, toggle and process retirement.

`tmux_pane:stop_pipe/1` closes the native connection and can discard pending
bytes. Wait for the consumer's acknowledgement before closing when delivery
matters. Closing does not kill or wait for an arbitrary shell process; a
consumer that does not finish on EOF needs application-level coordination.
`tmux_server:close/1` preserves the borrowed pane and its tmux-owned pipe.
[Jobs and operations](jobs.md) covers library-owned command clients;
[configuration and signals](configuration.md) explains native wait channels.

# Build and browse the native API

Core and workspace contracts live in Erlang `-moduledoc`, `-doc` and specs.
OTP's compiler stores EEP-48 documentation chunks; ExDoc renders searchable module,
function and type pages. Source links open captured files with line anchors
and content digests. An unchanged file also links to its exact Git commit;
changed files are labelled as working-tree previews.

Compile the project:

```console
$ mise exec -- rebar3 compile
```

Prepare the checksum-pinned ExDoc tool. This step uses the network:

```console
$ python3 tools/build_docs.py --prepare
```

Build the browser without fetching dependencies:

```console
$ mise exec -- python3 tools/build_docs.py
```

Open `_build/docs/core/index.html`. This is a local build, not a published
HexDocs URL. The build refreshes compiled modules before rendering. The
renderer treats warnings as failures and uses the OTP 29
build of ExDoc. It consumes compiler chunks directly because the older EDoc
source-extraction path rejects native-record attributes.

## Types at application boundaries

Entity constructors accept generated maps such as
`t:tmux_model:pane_input/0`. Required fields and scalar categories are visible
to Dialyzer. Optional observations retain `not_loaded` and `unavailable`;
nullable fields also accept `none`. Numeric fields accept integral floats,
which normalize to integers. Runtime validation checks bounds, ID syntax,
UTF-8 and derived values. Use `tmux_model:new/2` when validating dynamic maps
and handle its `t:tmux_schema:error_detail/0` result.

`t:tmux_select:t/1` describes the intended row type. Dialyzer in OTP 29.1.2
does not always substitute actual argument types into generic return
variables. For example, a selection passed through `tmux_select:one/1` can
lose its specific entity type during analysis. A successful analysis does
not prove every pane/window relationship. Keep native patterns and runtime
action validation at those boundaries. The
[OTP contract solver](https://github.com/erlang/otp/blob/OTP-29.1.2/lib/dialyzer/src/dialyzer_contracts.erl#L477-L502)
records this generic constraint limitation.

The installed-consumer outer check executes valid constructor calls and
requires Dialyzer to reject wrong Boolean/numeric fields and missing session
identity or window-link index. It analyzes the installed core outside the
umbrella; a green library analysis alone does not establish those diagnostics.

# Load a workspace file

Load desired sessions, windows and panes with `tmux_workspace:load/1`, then
inspect the normalized graph with `tmux_workspace:to_map/1`. The workspace
application depends on the core's public JSON API and OTP libraries.

This loader performs filesystem I/O. It does not contact tmux or launch the
programs in the file. Planning, applying changes and an installed workspace
CLI remain implementation work.

## Describe the desired graph

[This input file](../examples/workspace.json) declares one session, one window
and two panes. `endpoint` names a host-configured connection; it cannot choose
a socket. `argv` is literal executable data. `shell` explicitly requests shell
syntax for a future apply policy to authorize.

<!-- example-input: examples/workspace.json -->

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "id": "demo",
  "endpoint": "dev",
  "sessions": [
    {
      "name": "editor",
      "windows": [
        {
          "name": "api",
          "layout": "even-horizontal",
          "panes": [
            {"cwd": ".", "argv": ["rebar3", "shell"]},
            {"cwd": ".", "shell": "exec erl"}
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

Relative working directories use the canonical workspace file directory.
Symlinks resolve before `..`; directories must already exist. There is no
environment interpolation. Each pane requires exactly one launch form.

An explicit `id` keeps workspace identity stable when moving the file.
Otherwise the loader hashes its canonical filename. Optional entity `key`
fields identify sessions, windows and panes across edits. Without a key, the
loader uses the entry's JSON pointer; reordering entries changes identity.
Keys must be unique across the workspace.

## Read and inspect it

Compile this checkout first:

```console
$ mise exec -- rebar3 compile
```

Run the complete program below:

```console
$ mise exec -- escript tools/run_examples.escript workspace
```

The program copies the real JSON file to an owned temporary directory, checks
the desired object graph and canonical cwd, and verifies removal of its files.
The outer check repeats it using installed core and workspace OTP archives.

<!-- example: examples/workspace_demo.erl -->

```erlang
-module(workspace_demo).
-moduledoc "Load a real workspace file and inspect its desired object graph.".
-export([run/0]).

-spec run() -> map().
run() ->
    Suffix = binary:encode_hex(crypto:strong_rand_bytes(10), lowercase),
    Directory = <<"/tmp/ltm-workspace-demo-", Suffix/binary>>,
    ok = file:make_dir(Directory),
    Output = tmux_scope:run_or_error(fun() ->
        ok = file:change_mode(Directory, 8#700),
        Path = filename:join(Directory, <<"workspace.json">>),
        {ok, _} = file:copy("examples/workspace.json", Path),
        {ok, Workspace} = tmux_workspace:load(Path),
        #{id := Id, endpoint := Endpoint, sessions := [Session]} =
            tmux_workspace:to_map(Workspace),
        #{name := SessionName, windows := [Window]} = Session,
        #{name := WindowName, layout := <<"even-horizontal">>,
          panes := [Build, Shell]} = Window,
        #{cwd := Directory, launch := #{argv := Arguments}} = Build,
        [<<"rebar3">>, <<"shell">>] = Arguments,
        #{cwd := Directory, launch := #{shell := <<"exec erl">>}} = Shell,
        #{workspace_id => Id, endpoint => Endpoint,
          session => SessionName, window => WindowName, panes => 2,
          first_pane_key => maps:get(key, Build), canonical_cwd => true,
          shell_declared => true, launched => false}
    end, fun() ->
        ok = file:del_dir_r(Directory)
    end),
    {error, enoent} = file:read_file_info(Directory),
    Output#{files_removed => true}.
```

## Handle validation failures

Errors include a source basename, a `code` and a JSON `path` with zero-based
array indexes. Unknown fields, duplicate JSON object keys and duplicate
entity keys fail before any tmux operation. A pane with both launch forms
returns `ambiguous_launch`; a nonexistent directory returns `invalid_directory`.

The loader accepts version 1, at most 256 KiB of JSON and 32 nested
containers. Collections contain 1–64 entries and a workspace has at most
2048 entities. IDs and keys use at most 128 UTF-8 bytes; names use at most
256. Names exclude controls and backslashes; session names also exclude
periods and colons because tmux rewrites them. Launch argv has at most 256
elements and a 32 KiB aggregate bound. Layouts use the five standard named
tmux arrangements.

Local filesystem checks are synchronous and assume trusted directories.
They provide byte bounds and canonicalization, not a filesystem sandbox,
an I/O deadline or protection against concurrent replacement of path entries.
See the [API browser](api.md) for native types and
[project policy](project-policy.md) for application boundaries.

# Project policy

This port provides an Erlang core and a workspace consumer. An MCP package,
server or SDK integration is excluded from implementation and release scope.

The [architecture decision record](adr-0001-architecture.md) explains the
selected design, alternatives, consequences and conditions for reconsideration.

## OTP application boundaries

Develop the applications together in the Rebar3 umbrella. Each application is
an independent package boundary with its own metadata, license and changelog.

| Application | Responsibility | Library dependencies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `libtmux_erlang` | tmux transport, operations, domain objects, snapshots and queries | OTP applications |
| `libtmux_erlang_workspace` | JSON workspace loading, plans, apply and CLI | Public core API and OTP applications |

The workspace application declares its core dependency in its application
metadata. It uses public APIs through installed packages; source paths and
private core modules are not integration boundaries. The core is independent
of the workspace application. Additional core packages need their own reusable
responsibility and explicit consumer dependencies.

Package qualification must install each consumer outside the umbrella against
the produced core package. A successful umbrella build alone does not prove
that an independently installed workspace package works. The workspace CLI is

## Runtime dependencies

Use the latest stable Erlang/OTP baseline and native OTP facilities. Use OTP
JSON for documents and the standard argument parser for the planned CLI.
Prefer module functions, native records, specs, tagged results and supervised
processes where ownership requires them.

Keep Erlang runtime dependencies within OTP. An exception requires a concrete
capability need, maintenance assessment and recorded architecture decision.
Test, build and documentation tools are separate from runtime dependencies.

Support covers tmux 3.3a–3.8, including intermediate releases, on Linux x86_64
and arm64. CI uses only the latest stable Erlang/OTP release and samples the
oldest supported and newest stable tmux releases. Verify upstream releases
before updating the exact pins. Historical results retain their recorded scope.

The Linux transport uses the bundled C11 executable for bounded I/O and owned
process retirement. It is built from packaged source with recorded provenance.
Workspace code uses that transport through the public core API.

The layout follows [Rebar3 application organization](https://rebar3.org/docs/basic_usage/)
and [OTP application boundaries and dependencies](https://www.erlang.org/doc/system/applications.html).
